Chapter 6: The Mechanics of Morning
The futon didn’t feel like an alien landing site anymore. It just felt like a stiff mattress over tatami that needed airing out.

When I opened my eyes, the ceiling was the same pale plaster with the faint hairline fracture near the light fixture. The light filtering around the plastic edges of the roller blind was a thin, cold grey, tinted with the blue of an overcast six-thirty in early spring.

I lay there for a minute, letting my breathing settle into the room.

My shoulder blades pressed against the floor with less surface area than I was used to. That was still the first thing every morning—the sense of a revised perimeter. The frame under the blanket was narrow, light enough that shifting my hip bone against the cotton padding made a dull, precise point of pressure. My hair was caught under my left armpit. It was always caught somewhere now. When I rolled over, it dragged against the nape of my neck like a heavy, cool skein of silk, strands sticking to the corner of my mouth.

I blew them away, sat up, and ran both hands back through it.

Black hair, dense enough to hold water like a sponge, with that weird, stubborn dark-teal sheen whenever the light hit the grain sideways. It fell well past my collarbones now. In my old life, my hair had been thick, coarse, and trimmed every four weeks at a strip-mall barber who smelled of barbicide and menthol tobacco. Here, if I didn't gather it, it got into my eyes, my collar, the toast butter, everything.

I found a black elastic band on the low wooden table beside the lamp and tied it back behind my neck, pulling it tight until the skin around my temples lifted slightly.

The apartment was cold. The kind of concrete-box cold that seeped in through the balcony slider overnight. I got to my feet, my bare soles sticking faintly to the floorboards of the kitchen corridor, and turned the dial on the two-burner gas range. A blue circle of flame hissed into life with a heavy flump. I set a dented aluminum kettle over it, then walked into the narrow washroom to deal with my face.

The mirror over the plastic basin didn’t lie, but it still startled me if I looked too quickly.

Ira Lowe looked back.

Sixteen years old. Pale skin that seemed completely unacquainted with sunburn, resting over facial bones that were almost irritatingly tidy—a small, straight nose, jawline tapering into a rounded chin, lips that naturally sat in a faint, neutral line. And the eyes: vivid, high-saturation emerald green, rimmed by thick, dark lashes that looked like they belonged on a high-end department store cosmetics advert.

"Morning, stranger," I muttered.

The voice was soft. Not a squeak, but light, pitched high in the chest cavity, clear as a bell. It didn't sound like a boy who had spent seventeen years yelling across basketball courts and arguing over rusted mufflers. It sounded like a choir student who had never missed a Sunday service.

I grabbed the plastic toothbrush, loaded it with chalky mint paste, and scrubbed until my gums stung.

Today was the exam.

Yesterday had been the desperate reconnaissance mission—the panic of waking up inside someone else's skin, finding a foreign alien life stuffed into a shoebox apartment, fumbling through railway lines until I found the name Kuoh, and staring up at the stone gates of an academy that looked like it had been lifted from an architectural digest of Prussian palaces.

Today wasn't reconnaissance. Today was the actual door.

In the kitchen, the kettle whistled with a thin, wheezing shriek. I killed the burner, poured hot water into a chipped mug over a packet of instant drip coffee, and watched the dark foam bloom over the paper filter. The smell—roasted, bitter, slightly burnt chicory—helped more than anything else to anchor my skull to the room.

On the low table lay the brown envelope.

I sat down cross-legged, my knees clicking faintly, and checked the contents for the fourth time.

The application slip for Kuoh Academy. The official stamp in vermilion ink was square and crisp over the lower right corner. My passport-style photo was stapled to the top left: Ira looking dead at the lens with an expression of polite, vacant melancholy. My birth date. My registered address.

Next to the papers lay three pre-sharpened HB pencils, a soft plastic eraser still in its cardboard sleeve, a pencil sharpener shaped like a tiny metal wedge, and a worn black leather wallet containing eleven thousand yen in crisp, folded bills and a small handful of heavy silver hundred-yen coins.

Beside that was my phone. A silver Panasonic flip handset, scratched along the hinge, dead silent. In 2005, a phone was a tool for short text messages and quick calls, not an endless window into the collective panic of the planet. It sat on the table like a folded cigarette case. I slipped it into my coat pocket along with the wallet.

I dressed carefully.

There was no official uniform for applicants from independent or overseas schooling backgrounds, so I had to make do with what Ira’s tiny closet provided: a charcoal-grey wool duffel coat that hung slightly long past my knees, black tailored trousers that were an inch too wide in the waist—cinched tight with a stiff leather belt—and a plain white collared shirt under a navy-blue crewneck sweater.

The clothes smelled faintly of cedar and dry cleaning. When I pulled the coat on, the heavy wool settled against my shoulders with a reassuring weight. It hid the narrowness of my chest and the slender taper of my ribs. In a loose coat, at least, I looked less like an illustration and more like a person walking down a street to take a test.

I slid the envelope and stationery into a plain canvas shoulder bag, jammed my feet into a pair of scuffed black leather lace-ups at the genkan, and tied the double knots tight.

I took one breath of the apartment’s stale, heated air, turned the latch, and stepped out.

The outside was loud, bright, and smelled of wet bitumen.

The morning chill hit my face with the force of a cold wet towel. The sky above the apartment block was a vast, seamless apron of pale slate, stitched across by thousands of black utility cables that looped from concrete pole to concrete pole like drunken handwriting.

A small delivery van—a white Kei truck with a dented rear fender—rattled past down the two-lane street, its engine whining like an overgrown sewing machine. On the opposite corner, a woman in a quilted apron was rolling up the corrugated steel shutter of a dry cleaner's, the metal slats screaming against their rusted runners with a sharp clack-clack-clack that echoed between the three-story apartment fronts.

I turned left toward the station.

My feet found the pavement with a different stride than they used to. Ira’s legs were shorter than Jonah’s by maybe two inches, but his center of gravity was lower, cleaner. I didn't clomp. The leather soles made a crisp, polite tapping sound on the tarmac as I navigated the narrow strip between the roadside drainage ditch and the line of parked utility bicycles.

A middle-aged salaryman in a beige trench coat hurried past me, smelling of stale tobacco and hair tonic, his black briefcase swinging close to his knee. As he cut in front to avoid a puddle, his elbow brushed my sleeve.

"Ah, sumimasen," he muttered reflexively, barely looking down, dipping his head before marching on toward the station entrance.

The voice had carried that particular, automatic deference usually reserved for teenage girls or junior office clerks. I looked down at my coat, felt the strand of hair that had slipped free of the band tickling the edge of my jaw, and shoved my hands deep into my pockets.

Right. Don't worry about it. Just keep moving.

The station entrance was a gaping concrete mouth beneath the elevated tracks, swallowing an unbroken stream of commuters. The air inside smelled of ozone, damp wool, paper newsprint, and the sweet, fried-sugar reek of the waffle stand tucked beside the stairs.

I didn't have an automated Suica card yet—those were just starting to dominate the turnstiles—so I joined the short queue at the ticket vending machines. The mechanical clatter was relentless: buttons thunking inward, coins dropping into metal hoppers with a dull chink-chink, the sudden hiss of automated ticket gates snapping shut when someone mistimed their approach.

I looked at the fare map above the machine. It was a massive, spider-webbed acrylic diagram of coloured lines and black kanji.

Kuoh. Transfer at Minami-Chofu, take the private line outward.

I fed a thousand-yen note into the slot. The machine swallowed it with a hungry mechanical hum, clicked three times, and spat out a small, stiff paper ticket with a magnetic brown back, along with my change in heavy coins.

I took the ticket, walked to the turnstile, and slid it into the narrow slot. It vanished, the gate flashed a quiet green bulb, and the ticket popped out of the slot three feet ahead with a tiny snick. I snatched it mid-stride and joined the cattle drive up the concrete stairs toward Platform 3.

The wind on the elevated platform was biting. It smelled of steel brake dust and distant rain.

A train was already pulling in. The yellow-striped nose of the JR commuter train slid along the edge of the platform with a heavy, grinding squeal of iron on iron, the wind of its arrival flattening my coat against my shins. The double doors hissed open in unison, and the platform breathed out a wave of warm, humid, human air.

I squeezed into the middle carriage, finding a pocket of space between a vertical handrail and the back of a plastic seat bench.

The train lurched.

It wasn't a sudden jolt, but a massive, hydraulic displacement of mass that shoved everyone three inches to the left. The steel wheels under the floorboards began their rhythmic, hammering chant—ka-tunk, ka-tunk, ka-tunk—accelerating as the grey concrete of the platform gave way to a blur of brick walls, rooftop water tanks, and laundry flapping on narrow apartment balconies.

Sunlight broke through the cloud cover suddenly, cutting diagonally through the smeared glass of the train windows.

It was blinding. The light caught every micro-scratch in the acrylic glass, transforming the window into a fractured sheet of pale gold. It struck the commuters opposite me: the sharp, white crease of a starched collar; the fine, dusty texture of an older woman's wool scarf; the blue-black shine of school uniforms.

Directly across from me, holding the leather strap above her head, stood a woman who looked to be in her mid-twenties.

She wasn't an anime character. She didn't have lavender hair or an impossible waist. But she was undeniably, startlingly striking in the way only real, well-put-together people are on an otherwise miserable morning commute.

She wore a sharply tailored camel-wool coat over an ivory silk blouse, the collar open just enough to show the hollow of her throat and a thin silver chain. Her skirt was dark, cut just above the knee, revealing legs in sheer, dark-tinted stockings that ended in glossy black leather heels planted firmly against the ribbed rubber flooring of the train. Her hair was rich, chestnut-brown, gathered into an effortless loose twist at the back of her head, with soft, curled tendrils framing high cheekbones and a mouth painted in a quiet, berry-red gloss.

She was holding a paperback novel with one hand, her long, manicured fingers turning the thin page without looking down.

As the train took a long, banked curve over a river bridge, the whole carriage leaned. Her shoulder brushed mine gently—just a soft, warm bump of wool against wool.

A scent came with it. Not heavy perfume, but something crisp and floral—expensive citrus, clean soap, and the faint, bitter edge of black tea.

I caught myself looking. Not even subtly. My brain, which had spent seventeen years as an awkward teenage boy, was currently firing off all the standard, embarrassing alerts. She had that effortless, adult composure that made sixteen-year-old boys feel like they were made of wooden sticks and grease.

Then she glanced down from her book.

Her eyes were hazel, sharp, and slightly tired around the corners. She caught me staring.

I froze, my jaw locking, my internal Jonah desperately preparing for the cold, disgusted glare every teenage boy deserves when he's caught ogling a commuter twice his social bracket.

Instead, her expression softened.

She looked at my face—really looked at it—and her lips curved into a tiny, amused, almost maternal smile.

"Are you all right?" she asked. Her voice was low, smooth, cutting easily through the rumble of the train. "You look pale. Is it an exam day?"

She was looking at my canvas bag, the pencil case visible through the unzipped top edge.

"Uh," I said.

My voice came out light, slightly breathless, and high.

"Yeah," I managed, clearing my throat and trying to drop the pitch half an octave. It didn't drop much. "Entrance test."

"I thought so," she said, her smile widening just enough to crinkle the skin near her eyes. She shifted her grip on the overhead strap, giving me another three inches of breathing room against the wall. "Don't be nervous. With a face like that, the interviewers will probably pass you before you even sit down. Do your best, okay?"

She gave me a gentle, conspiratorial nod, then looked back down at her paperback, turning the page with a clean flick of her thumb.

I stared at the floorboards between my boots.

My face was burning. It was burning hot enough to fry an egg on my forehead.

She hadn't thought I was a creep. She had looked at me, seen a pretty, fragile, nervous girl in an oversized coat heading off to a high school entrance exam, and decided to offer some big-sister encouragement.

Jesus Christ.

I pinched the bridge of my nose, feeling the delicate, narrow bone beneath the skin. This is my life now. I am officially non-threatening. I am an ornament.

The train began to brake, the air compressors under the chassis sighing loudly as the automated voice chimed: “Next stop, Minami-Chofu. Minami-Chofu. Doors will open on the left side.”

The woman closed her book with a quiet thwip, slipped it into her leather handbag, and stepped toward the opening doors without looking back. I let the crowd carry me out onto the platform behind her, the crisp morning wind immediately clearing the citrus scent from my head.

The transfer concourse was an underground concrete cavern, smelling of damp tile and grease.

I had forty minutes before the registration window opened at Kuoh, and my stomach was suddenly, aggressively hollow. That cup of instant coffee had burned away into pure stomach acid.

Beside the stairs to the private railway platforms was a small, glowing kiosk—a kiosk with a red canvas awning and an aluminum warming cabinet displaying rows of hot canned beverages and paper-wrapped buns.

"One pork bun, please," I said, stepping up to the waist-high counter.

The old man behind the glass had a white paper cap and hands like wrinkled butcher paper. He didn't look at me for more than a second. "One-twenty."

I handed him two hundred-yen coins. He used metal tongs to lift a steaming, paper-bottomed nikuman from the wire rack inside the steamer, dropped it into a thin plastic wrapper, and pushed it across the stainless-steel counter with my eighty yen in change.

"Watch out, it's hot," he grunted.

It was. The bun was scorching against the palm of my hand, the thick white dough soft, yielding, and smelling intensely of steamed yeast, ginger, and braised pork.

I stepped into a corner out of the pedestrian flow, leaning against a square concrete pillar covered in faded posters for 2005 cinema releases—some local drama, an animated film, a domestic thriller—and peeled back the paper base.

The first bite tore open the steam pocket. Hot, salty broth hit my tongue, followed by the rich, fatty chew of minced pork, green onions, and sweet soy.

I chewed slowly, watching the boots and shoes churn past.

It was good. It was stupidly, miraculously good. In my old life, breakfast had been dry cereal eaten standing over the sink while watching the kitchen clock tick toward seven-fifteen. Here, standing under an underground transit ceiling in a town whose name I still had to double-check on my ticket, the pork fat and steam felt like the only completely solid things in the universe.

I swallowed, took a second bite, and let the warmth settle into the pit of my ribs.

I wasn't a ghost anymore. Ghosts don't have to digest pork.

The private line out to Kuoh was different.

The train was shorter—only four cars—and the commuters were no longer the grey, hurried salarymen of central Tokyo. There were more students here, kids in dark navy blazers with polished brass buttons, older women carrying woven shopping baskets, and local tradesmen with canvas tool wraps tucked under their arms.

I almost blew the transfer.

At the platform divide, the overhead signage split into two arrows: one for the Local, one for the Rapid. In my head, Rapid meant faster, which meant better. I had one foot over the threshold of the Rapid car when I glanced at the small, paper timetable posted on the carriage door.

Kuoh: Passed.

The Rapid bypassed it entirely. Kuoh wasn't a major hub; it was an affluent suburb, a dead-end pocket of green that the express trains ignored on their way to the industrial coast.

I yanked my foot back just as the warning chime sounded, the rubber edge of the closing door catching the tail of my coat with a faint thump.

A group of junior high boys on the platform snickered behind their hands.

"Stupid," I muttered to myself, stepping back toward the wooden benches. My heart was thumping in my throat. Not panic—just the cold, sharp adrenaline of a near-miss.

I didn't freeze, though. I didn't sit down and wait for someone to save me. I walked over to the pillar, studied the blue Local timetable, confirmed the arrival time of the next train—seven minutes—and stood right behind the yellow line with my hands in my pockets, breathing evenly through my nose.

You fix the problem. You don't whine about the track.

When the Local train arrived, it was half-empty.

The seats were covered in faded green velour that puffed a faint cloud of dust when I sat down. As the train cleared the concrete trench of the station, the city began to unravel.

The transition wasn't cinematic; it was gradual, mundane, and vast. The concrete office towers shrank into five-story brick apartment buildings, which gave way to narrow streets of two-story detached homes with tiled roofs and tiny, immaculate carports holding boxy silver hatchbacks.

Then came the greenery.

It wasn't wild forest. It was managed, wealthy Japanese suburbia: massive, dark-green zelkova trees leaning over high concrete walls; bamboo groves tucked between modern residential developments; wide, clean asphalt avenues lined with ginkgo trees whose bare branches reached up toward the clearing sky like grey bone.

The light changed. Out here, away from the glass canyons of the city center, the morning sky felt huge. The grey cloud deck was breaking apart into long, torn ribbons of white, letting down broad, brilliant pillars of pale gold sunlight that washed over the rooftops.

The automated speaker chimed with a clear, two-tone bell:

“Kuoh. Kuoh. Please check that you have not left any belongings behind.”

Kuoh Station didn't look like an annex of Tokyo. It looked like an old European railway depot that had been meticulously rebuilt by Japanese civil engineers.

The roof was a dark vaulted iron framework set with frosted glass panes, letting the morning light fall across clean, brick-paved platforms. There was no trash. There were no cigarette butts crushed into the expansion joints. Even the air smelled different—cooler, carrying a sharp, clean scent of cedarwood, damp moss, and mountain earth that seemed to drift down from the low, forested ridges that hemmed the town in from the north.

I walked out through the wicket, slipped my used ticket into the collection box, and stood on the station forecourt.

The town of Kuoh sloped upward.

Wide streets paved in smooth, dark tarmac wound gently up the hill, flanked by broad stone sidewalks, wrought-iron streetlamps that looked like they belonged in nineteenth-century Vienna, and high, whitewashed perimeter walls that concealed sprawling residential estates.

And at the top of that gentle rise, dominating the entire district like an ancient fortress converted into a sanctuary, was Kuoh Academy.

From this distance, the scale was clearer than it had been yesterday. The main building was a massive, three-story neo-classical structure of pale, cream-coloured stone, capped with high mansard roofs of weathered slate. Flanking it were modern extensions—glass-fronted wings and broad athletic pavilions—all connected by covered stone colonnades that cut through immaculately kept lawns.

It was intimidating as hell.

It wasn't a high school. It was an institution. It had the heavy, silent gravity of money so old that it didn't need to brag about itself.

I adjusted the strap of my canvas bag, pulled my collar against the wind, and began the walk up the hill.

The approach road was already busy.

Groups of applicants were moving in the same direction, easy to spot by their nervous posture and their plain, dark junior-high blazers. Some were accompanied by mothers in modest wool coats and pearls; others walked alone, clutching their plastic document folders like shields.

Then there were the actual Kuoh students.

The academy had only recently transitioned from an elite, ultra-traditional all-girls private school into a co-educational institution. That much I had gleaned from the paperwork yesterday. But seeing it in the flesh was another matter.

The current female students—the second- and third-years—wore uniforms that were frankly absurd in their attention to detail: high-waisted black skirts with white frilled trim, white shirts under tailored black vests with crimson ribbon ties, and long black capes that fluttered around their calves as they walked. They moved in tight, quiet clusters, their voices low and musical, ignoring the applicants with the casual, devastating indifference of people who already owned the ground they walked on.

I passed beneath the massive wrought-iron front gates.

The ironwork was black, spiked, and bore a complex crest in the center—two intertwined wings resting over an open book and a stylized sword. The gravel on the main approach crunch-crunched under hundreds of leather soles, a rhythmic, oceanic sound that filled the broad avenue between the double rows of ancient cherry trees.

The buds on the branches were still tight, dark nodules, not yet ready to burst. It was too early for blossoms.

"Applicants for General Studies, please proceed to the West Hall entrance!"

The voice came through a handheld megaphone, flat, slightly distorted, but completely authoritative.

Standing on the low stone steps of the administrative wing was a folding table covered in green baize. Behind it stood three teachers in dark suits, alongside several older students wearing white armbands marked with the school crest.

I joined the line.

The boy in front of me was trembling slightly. I could see the fine, rapid vibration of his coat hem. He was gripping an envelope so hard that his knuckles were white, his eyes fixed on the stone pavers between his boots.

I looked past him, watching the machinery of the place work.

The registration was fast, efficient, and cold. You stepped up, presented your examination slip, an administrator checked your name against a thick, leather-bound register, an older student handed you a printed plastic desk card with your exam number, and you were directed into the holding area.

"Next," one of the teachers called out.

The trembling boy stepped forward, bowed too low, fumbled his paperwork onto the baize, and stammered his name. The teacher, an older man with wire-rimmed glasses and a thin grey mustache, didn't even look up as he inked a red seal onto the boy's form.

"Second floor, Lecture Room 2B. Move along."

The boy scrambled off like he had been granted a reprieve from an execution.

I stepped up to the green baize.

The wind caught my duffel coat, pulling the front open slightly. I reached into my canvas bag, drew out the brown envelope, and laid the stamped form flat on the cloth.

"Ira Lowe," I said.

My voice was clear. It didn't waver.

The teacher paused. His pen hovered an inch above the paper. He looked up, his small, dark eyes resting first on the name printed in roman letters, then drifting up to my face.

He didn't say anything for two seconds. He just looked at the pale skin, the emerald eyes, the long black hair tied back against the collar of the duffel coat. His eyebrows twitched together in a tiny, almost imperceptible knot of confusion before his gaze dropped back to the gender box on the form.

Male.

He cleared his throat, a dry, abrasive rattle.

"Overseas transfer track?" he asked, his tone shifting from bored routine to something faintly cautious.

"Independent curriculum," I replied evenly. "Everything is in the dossier."

He dipped his seal into the vermilion paste, pressed it firmly against the corner of the slip with a sharp, heavy thunk, and slid a blue plastic placard across the baize toward me.

Applicant No. 1044.

"Third floor, North Hall, Room 301," he said. He didn't smile, but his eyes lingered on me as I picked up the placard. "Pencils and erasers only on the desks. Bags in the rear cubbies. The examination begins at nine sharp."

"Understood. Thank you."

I took the card, gave a shallow, polite bow, and turned toward the wide stone archway of the main hall.

The interior of Kuoh Academy was dead quiet compared to the courtyard.

The floors were polished parquetry—dark, honey-coloured oak laid in a herringbone pattern that gleamed under the high, arched windows. The walls were panelled in dark mahogany up to waist height, topped with white plaster that smelled faintly of old floor wax, chalk, and lime.

As I walked down the central corridor toward the grand staircase, the crowd of applicants began to thin, channeled off into different wings by student guides.

That was where the foot traffic shifted.

It wasn't noisy; it was an absence. A dozen paces ahead of me, the center line of the corridor simply emptied out. People didn't scramble, but they moved aside early, stepping toward the wainscoting before she even reached the junction. Two senior boys who had been speaking in low, rushed murmurs leaned back against the wall, their chatter cutting off mid-sentence, their hands falling straight to their seams. A faculty member—a man with greying hair in a dark, tailored three-piece suit—stood half a pace behind her, waiting with a dark ledger pressed against his chest.

She was standing near the foot of the west gallery archway.

She was tall—several inches taller than the body I was wearing—with a slender, clean verticality to her frame that made her posture seem architectural rather than rigid. Her uniform was the academy's black and crimson, but it hung without a fold or wrinkle out of place. Her hair was cut into a jaw-length bob of midnight black, sheared in a line so straight against the pale skin of her neck that it looked measured with a rule.

She wore square-framed spectacles with thin dark wire rims resting on a narrow, delicate nose. Her features had an unusual, severe symmetry—the transition from cheekbone to chin drawn so cleanly that my eye hesitated trying to process it. She didn't look sick or cold, despite the morning frost outside; her skin had the smooth, untouched finish of fine marble.

The faculty member offered a slim leather folder, his voice kept low. "The third-tier annex registers have been finalized, but if the arrival numbers from the eastern rail link require an extension—"

"No," she said.

Her voice was quiet, dry, and unhurried. It carried cleanly through the hall without being raised.

"The railway schedule was published six weeks in advance," she said. "Those who fail to anticipate municipal maintenance lack the fundamental discipline Kuoh requires. Close the registry at eight-forty-five."

"Understood," the man murmured. He lowered his gaze and stepped back half a pace without an ounce of friction.

She closed the folder with a light, deliberate movement of her fingers.

As she turned toward the corridor, the high clerestory windows caught her profile.

And right then, my eyes caught something wrong on the floor.

The morning sun was cutting diagonally through the glass, throwing long slashes of light across the honey-coloured parquetry. As she shifted her footing, her shadow fell across the oak planks toward the wall.

It was too long.

For half a heartbeat, the dark shape cast by her hem and shoulders reached five or six inches past where the geometry of the window mullions should have allowed—a sharp, heavy blade of grey that seemed to cling to the timber with an unnatural density.

I blinked.

When my eyes focused again, the floor was ordinary. Just a pale grey shadow resting over the wood grain, angled exactly with the light. A trick of the double-paned leaded glass and the morning glare.

Then her chin lifted, and her gaze swept the hall.

Behind her glasses, her eyes were a dark, deep violet.

They moved across the students until they reached me.

At close range, her eye line sat clearly above mine, but she didn't tilt her head. Her gaze simply lowered by a fraction of an inch. It paused on the blue placard gripped in my hand, moved to my duffel coat, and then to my face.

Her expression didn't change. The line of her mouth remained completely still.

Then her eyes moved on, continuing down the length of the corridor as if she had simply registered another piece of furniture.

She turned toward the western administrative wing. Her shoes made almost no sound against the parquet. The students against the wall didn't resume walking until the hem of her dark cape cleared the archway, and only then did the quiet shuffle and murmur of the hallway return.

I stood there for three seconds, the cold plastic edge of Applicant No. 1044 pressing into the meat of my palm.

Who was that?

The question had no answer, and I didn't have time to look for one. The older teacher had bowed to her like she owned the building, and my eyes were apparently playing tricks on me with the morning light.

I shook my head once, clearing the visual residue, and exhaled through my teeth.

Not your concern. Pass the exam first.

I found the central staircase—a massive, sweeping flight of marble steps with a polished brass banister—and began the climb to the third floor.

Room 301 was a high-ceilinged lecture hall with five tiers of long wooden desks, each equipped with an inkwell slot and a brass numbering plate.

The room smelled of dry radiator heat and cold slate. Sunlight was pouring through four massive, ten-foot-tall sash windows along the north wall, illuminating the millions of dust motes dancing in the quiet air.

There were about thirty applicants already seated. Nobody was talking. The silence was heavy, thick, and suffocating, punctuated only by the dry, occasional cough of a nervous kid or the faint, nervous rattle of a wooden pencil against a desktop.

I walked down the stepped aisle to the middle tier, found desk forty-four, and slid into the bench.

The wood of the desk was old, scarred by decades of ballpoint pens and compass points, polished down by hundreds of forearms until it felt as smooth as river stone. I took my three pencils from the bag, lined them up parallel to the brass number plate, placed the eraser beside them, and set the blue placard upright in the slot provided.

Then I took off my duffel coat, folded it over the back of the wooden bench, and sat down.

My canvas bag went into the wooden cubby under the seat.

I was alone with the pencils.

I leaned back against the uprights of the bench, folded my hands in my lap, and looked out the third-floor window.

From up here, the view was vast.

You could see over the slate roofs of the academy's outbuildings, past the high stone perimeter wall, and down into the sprawling green basin of Kuoh. The town looked peaceful, orderly, and entirely unaware of whatever machinery kept it running. Beyond the houses, the dark, pine-covered hills rolled upward into the pale blue morning, their ridges sharp against the horizon.

My chest felt strange.

Not tight. Not panicked.

Just... still.

Yesterday, I had been a dead boy who woke up in a terrifying, foreign cage, running on pure, frantic instinct, desperately looking for an address that made sense. I had been terrified that the world would realize I was an imposter, that some invisible referee would blow a whistle, grab me by the scruff of my neck, and drag me back into the dark where Jonah Laurence belonged.

That hadn't happened.

The train had taken my money. The woman on the commute had given me a gentle smile. The old man at the kiosk had handed me a pork bun. The administrator at the gate had stamped my paper.

The world didn't care who I had been. The world was too busy moving forward. It just saw a boy named Ira Lowe who had managed to find a coat, buy a ticket, and climb the hill to take a test.

I looked down at my hands.

The fingers were long, pale, and narrow. The knuckles were clean, completely unscarred. They didn't look like my hands. They never would.

Fine, I thought. Then they're mine now.

At the front of the lecture hall, the heavy oak door swung open with a dry, mechanical creak.

A proctor in a dark charcoal suit walked in, carrying a thick stack of sealed brown paper folios bound with red string. Behind him, another teacher carried an armful of wooden clipboards.

The proctor didn't look at us. He walked to the wide mahogany lectern, set the folios down with a heavy, final thwack, and drew a silver pocket watch from his waistcoat.

He clicked the watch open, checked the face, and looked up at the wall clock above the blackboard.

The long black second hand was sweeping upward, ticking through the final quadrant of the dial.

Eight-fifty-nine.

Every kid in the room seemed to stop breathing at the same time. The silence in the hall became absolute—so dense that I could hear the faint, high-frequency hiss of the steam radiator under the window and the sound of my own pulse tapping against my temples.

I reached out, picked up the first HB pencil, and felt the sharp, six-sided cedar casing settle against the middle finger of my right hand.

Above our heads, high in the central tower of the academy, the great iron bell began to swing.

The sound arrived first as a low, physical vibration through the floorboards—a deep, resonant hum that rattled the loose glass in the tall sash windows—before the actual chime struck.

GONG.

A massive, bronze, two-tone strike that rolled out across the slate roofs, echoing over the courtyard and out into the valley below.

The proctor snapped his pocket watch shut with a sharp click.

"It is nine o'clock," he said.

His voice was entirely devoid of drama. He reached for the red string on the first folio, snapped it with a single, practiced tug, and began to separate the papers.

"The examination will now begin."

Chapter Five — A Second Morning
“What the fuck?”

I stared at the mirror.

For several seconds, I couldn't make myself look away.

The person standing in front of me was still there, breathing when I breathed, shifting when I shifted. The reflection wasn't distorted. There was no strange light in the glass, no dreamlike haze, nothing that could explain what I was seeing.

It was just a mirror.

And somehow that made it worse.

I turned my head toward the room.

The bedroom looked exactly as it had a moment ago.

Morning light had begun to filter through the curtains, though I hadn't noticed it until then. It fell across the wooden floor in pale rectangles, catching the edges of the furniture and leaving the corners in softer shadow. The walls were a muted cream colour that changed subtly depending on where the sunlight touched them. A desk sat beneath the window, a chair tucked underneath it. There was a wardrobe against the opposite wall and a narrow shelf crowded with books.

Nothing about it looked supernatural.

That bothered me.

I looked toward the window.

The curtains moved slightly from the air coming through the gap. Beyond them I could see the tops of buildings and a strip of pale sky. A road ran somewhere below. I could hear a car passing, followed by the muffled sound of somebody talking.

Normal.

Everything sounded normal.

I looked back at the mirror.

The stranger was still looking at me.

I stepped closer.

He did the same.

My heart was beating too quickly.

I raised my right hand and slowly touched my cheek.

The reflection did exactly the same.

My fingers met warm skin.

I pulled them away.

Then I touched my face again, more carefully this time.

The shape was wrong.

Not wrong in the sense that anything was physically malformed. It was simply not my face.

The jaw was narrower than mine had been. The cheeks were softer. The eyes were much larger, framed by dark lashes that looked ridiculous when I remembered my own face.

And the hair—

Jesus Christ.

It was long.

Far too long.

Black at first glance, but with dark teal running through it and brighter green-blue colour underneath whenever the light caught it. It fell past my shoulders and continued down my back, thick enough that I couldn't understand how anybody was supposed to manage it every morning.

I reached behind myself and gathered some of it in one hand.

It was real.

I let it fall.

The weight of it brushed against my back.

I looked down at the clothes I was wearing.

They were unfamiliar too. Loose enough to hide most of my shape, but they couldn't hide the fact that the body itself was much smaller and more delicate than mine had been.

I looked around the room again.

There was a bed behind me.

A pair of shoes near it.

A school bag on the floor.

Several books on the desk.

A folded shirt.

A glass of water beside the bed.

Ordinary things.

Someone lived here.

Someone had been living here.

Someone whose room I was standing in.

The thought made my stomach turn.

I walked over to the desk.

There were notebooks stacked beside a few textbooks, all written in Japanese. I recognized enough of the writing to know what it was, but not enough to understand everything at a glance.

I picked one up.

The handwriting was neat.

Very neat.

I flipped through several pages.

Schoolwork.

Notes.

Dates.

Nothing immediately useful.

I put it back.

My eyes moved around the room again.

There was no photograph.

No family picture.

No obvious name written anywhere.

Nothing that immediately told me who this person was.

I checked the wardrobe.

Clothes.

Most of them looked expensive without being flashy. Everything was arranged more neatly than I would have expected from a teenager.

I opened a drawer.

Nothing.

Another.

Still nothing.

I stood there for a while.

My hands were beginning to shake.

I looked at them.

They were not my hands.

That thought landed differently this time.

Not abstractly.

Not like the mirror.

These were literally my hands now.

I flexed my fingers.

The movement felt natural.

Too natural.

That scared me more than if they had felt foreign.

I walked back toward the mirror.

“Okay.”

My voice came out soft.

I froze.

I tried again.

“Okay.”

The same voice.

It wasn't merely higher than mine.

It was genuinely soft. Feminine enough that if I'd heard it from another room, I wouldn't have assumed it belonged to a boy.

I stared at the mirror.

“No.”

My voice answered me from the room.

I swallowed.

“No, no, no.”

I sounded like somebody else.

I pressed both hands against my face.

This couldn't be happening.

I had died.

I remembered that much.

I remembered the feeling of everything disappearing.

I remembered the strange place afterward.

The stars.

The impossible spaces.

The feeling of moving through something far larger than anything I could understand.

And then this.

A room.

A body.

A life that wasn't mine.

I lowered my hands.

The mirror waited.

I thought about calling someone.

Then I realized I didn't know anyone here.

I thought about leaving.

Then I realized I didn't know where I was.

I thought about going back.

There was nowhere to go back to.

That was the thought that finally broke through everything else.

My old room was gone.

My house was gone.

My parents were gone.

My friends were gone.

School was gone.

Everything I'd complained about for years was suddenly something I couldn't have back.

The realization hit so hard that I had to sit down.

I sat on the edge of the bed and stared at the floor.

For a while, I didn't think anything.

Then everything came at once.

What had happened?

Was I dead?

Was this some kind of afterlife?

Was I dreaming?

If I was dreaming, why could I feel the floor beneath my feet?

If I was dead, why did I still remember everything?

If I wasn't dead, where was I?

Who was this person?

Why was I in his body?

Why did the room look like somebody else's life?

Why did I have no idea what was going on?

What happened to my parents?

Would they know I was dead?

Would they think I'd run away?

Would somebody find me?

Would there even be a body?

I squeezed my eyes shut.

No.

Don't think about that.

Think about something else.

Anything else.

The room.

The desk.

The window.

The books.

The—

My old school.

I remembered sitting there.

I remembered people complaining about teachers.

I remembered the stupid things Daniel used to say.

I remembered my mother's voice from the kitchen.

I remembered my phone.

My bed.

My clothes.

The stupid crack in the ceiling.

All those ordinary things I'd never thought I'd miss.

I opened my eyes.

The room was still here.

The sun had climbed higher.

Morning was continuing without me.

People were going to work.

Students were probably going to school.

Somebody was probably already late.

The world had continued.

Mine hadn't.

I looked down at my hands again.

For some reason, that made me want to cry.

I didn't at first.

I just sat there.

Then my eyes started burning.

I rubbed them.

That only made it worse.

“Come on.”

My voice cracked.

I laughed once.

It wasn't funny.

I covered my face.

The tears came properly after that.

I tried to stop them.

I couldn't.

I cried because I didn't know where I was.

I cried because I didn't know whose body I was wearing.

I cried because I remembered being seventeen and thinking I still had plenty of time to figure things out.

I cried because there were so many stupid things I'd complained about that suddenly seemed unbelievably valuable.

I would have taken another boring morning.

Another argument.

Another embarrassing day at school.

Another night lying awake with my phone beside me.

I would have taken all of it.

I would have taken the parts of my life I'd hated if it meant I could have my life back.

At some point I lay down.

I don't remember exactly when I stopped crying.

I remember the room becoming darker.

I remember pulling the blanket around myself.

I remember thinking that tomorrow I would figure something out.

That thought was probably the only thing keeping me conscious.

Tomorrow.

I'd figure it out tomorrow.

I had to.

Eventually, exhaustion won.

I slept.

When I woke again, sunlight was already filling the room.

For a moment I didn't remember.

Then I opened my eyes.

The ceiling was unfamiliar.

I stared at it.

Then I remembered everything.

I closed my eyes again.

“Right.”

My voice was still wrong.

I opened them.

The morning looked different from the night.

The room no longer felt like a strange place I'd accidentally wandered into. Sunlight reached almost everywhere now, revealing small details I'd missed before. The walls had a warm cream tone. The wooden floor had faint scratches near the desk and darker marks where furniture had been moved. Dust showed itself in the light near the window, drifting lazily through the air.

There was something strangely comforting about that.

It was just a room.

A very unfamiliar room.

But a room.

I sat up.

My hair fell over my shoulder and nearly into my face.

I grabbed it.

“Oh, come on.”

I pulled it back and looked at the enormous amount of hair gathered in my hands.

Who had this much hair?

I stood up.

My legs felt slightly different from what I was used to. Lighter. The balance was different too, though I couldn't explain exactly how.

I took a few steps around the room.

My body adjusted quickly.

That was unsettling.

I wasn't consciously remembering how to walk.

It already knew.

I stopped.

My body knew things I didn't.

I didn't know what that meant.

I decided not to think about it yet.

The bathroom was across the hall.

I found it after opening the wrong door first.

That seemed about right.

Inside, everything was clean and ordinary. White tile, a small sink, a mirror above it, towels folded neatly beside the shower. Morning light came through the frosted window and turned the room almost golden.

I stared at my reflection again.

There was no darkness to hide behind now.

I looked like a girl.

Not exactly.

But enough that if somebody saw me from a distance, I wasn't sure they'd know.

I leaned closer.

The face was almost delicate.

Large green eyes.

Fine eyebrows.

Long lashes.

A small nose.

Soft lips.

Pale skin with a warm flush through the cheeks.

I touched my face.

“Seriously?”

I turned sideways.

That did not help.

The body was extremely slender. Narrow shoulders. Thin arms. Small waist. Long legs.

Nothing about it looked masculine in the way I was used to seeing myself.

I looked down.

Then back at the mirror.

I was male.

I stared for several seconds.

“...Oh.”

I looked again.

Then away.

Then back.

The fact hadn't changed.

I rubbed my face.

This was ridiculous.

I'd spent the entire night trying to understand how I'd ended up in another person's body, and somehow I'd completely avoided dealing with the obvious part.

I wasn't in my body.

This body was male.

It just happened to look like this.

I stared at myself again.

For a brief moment, irritation washed over me.

Why did I have to look like this?

Why couldn't I have woken up looking normal?

Why did I have to deal with people mistaking me for a girl on top of everything else?

I ran a hand through my hair.

Then stopped.

The hair was actually beautiful.

That annoyed me.

I looked at my reflection.

The eyes were beautiful too.

The face was beautiful.

The whole body was...

Elegant.

I hated that I couldn't argue with it.

I looked down again.

“Wait.”

I stared.

Then looked at the mirror.

Then down again.

“...I have a dick.”

I stood there for another moment.

For some reason, that was reassuring.

At least I hadn't woken up as somebody completely different in every possible sense.

I was still a guy.

I just looked nothing like one.

I covered my face.

“Damn.”

I dropped my hands.

“Damn. I got reincarnated as a fucking femboy.”

I waited for the universe to punish me for saying it.

Nothing happened.

I looked back at the mirror.

“At least I look elegant.”

I immediately felt stupid.

Then I almost laughed.

Almost.

The tension in my chest loosened slightly.

That mattered.

I turned toward the shower.

I needed to wash.

After everything that had happened, taking a shower was probably the most normal thing I could do.

The water was warm.

Steam gathered slowly against the mirror while I stood beneath it, and for the first time since waking up, I wasn't trying to solve my entire existence.

I just stood there.

Water ran through my hair and down my shoulders.

I closed my eyes.

The old life came back.

Not as sharply as the night before.

Just pieces.

My room.

My school.

People I knew.

Things I had wanted to do.

Things I'd been angry about.

Things I'd planned to fix.

Later.

That word felt strange now.

I'd spent so much time assuming there would always be one.

Another day.

Another week.

Another chance.

Maybe this was one.

The thought came quietly.

I opened my eyes.

Steam blurred the room around me.

Maybe this was a second chance.

I didn't know why.

I didn't know who had given it to me.

I didn't even know if it was a gift.

But I was alive.

Whatever else was true, I was alive.

And if I was alive, then maybe I could do something with that.

The thought didn't erase everything.

I still missed home.

I still didn't understand what had happened.

I still didn't know whose life I had fallen into.

But for the first time since the mirror, those questions didn't feel like the only things in the world.

I turned the water off.

I dried myself, got dressed, and went back into the bedroom.

The morning felt different.

Not happier.

Just possible.

Finding information turned out to be easier once I stopped looking for some grand explanation.

The apartment had plenty of ordinary evidence.

A wallet was in the top drawer of the desk.

Inside were several bills, coins, a few cards and an identification document.

I pulled it out.

The name printed on it stopped me.

Ira Lowe.

I read it again.

Ira Lowe.

That was the name of the person whose life I had apparently stepped into.

I sat down.

“Ira.”

The name felt strange in my head.

I tried saying it.

“Ira Lowe.”

My voice made the name sound softer than I expected.

I looked at the document again.

There was an age.

Sixteen.

I stared.

“Sixteen?”

That explained some things.

Not everything.

But enough.

The body was younger than I was.

Or had been.

I put the document down.

Nothing happened.

No childhood memories appeared.

No faces.

No voice whispered inside my head.

There was just the name.

Ira Lowe.

That was all I had.

I searched through the desk more carefully.

There were school papers.

Letters.

A timetable.

A few textbooks.

Eventually I found an envelope with a school crest printed on the front.

I opened it.

The letter inside was an admission notice.

I read it twice.

Then a third time.

Kuoh Academy.

I sat back.

Kuoh.

I'd never heard of it.

There was a date near the bottom.

The entrance examination was tomorrow.

I stared at the page.

“Tomorrow?”

I checked the date again.

Tomorrow.

I looked around the room.

Then back at the letter.

“So I'm sixteen, apparently named Ira Lowe, living in an apartment I don't remember, and I'm supposed to take an entrance exam tomorrow.”

I leaned back in the chair.

“Great.”

At least this was a problem I understood.

School.

School had rules.

Tests had questions.

Questions had answers.

I could work with that.

The problem was getting there.

The address on the letter wasn't close enough to walk.

I found a printed map folded inside one of the drawers.

It was old-fashioned by the standards I remembered, but it worked. Streets, railway lines, districts and city names were printed clearly across the paper.

I traced the route with my finger.

There was a train station within walking distance.

From there, I could get toward Kuoh.

I checked the money in the wallet.

Enough.

Probably.

I hoped.

Then another thought occurred to me.

I didn't even know where the station was.

The first part of the journey was surprisingly normal.

I locked the apartment behind me and stood outside for a moment.

The street was already awake.

Cars moved through the intersection at the end of the road. Bicycles slipped between pedestrians. Shop shutters were being lifted one by one. A delivery truck was parked halfway across the street while two men stood beside it, apparently disagreeing about where something was supposed to go.

The morning smelled like warm pavement, food and faint exhaust.

Somewhere nearby, oil crackled in a pan.

A bicycle bell rang.

A radio played from inside one of the shops.

The sunlight reflected off windows and car roofs, throwing little flashes across the street whenever something moved.

It was busy without being chaotic.

I walked with the map folded in one hand.

Every few minutes I checked it.

Then the street.

Then the map again.

The first time, I thought I was doing well.

The second time, I realized I was going in the wrong direction.

I stopped beside a vending machine and unfolded the map.

The station was supposed to be southeast.

I looked down the road.

Nothing about it looked southeast.

I turned the map.

That didn't help.

I turned it again.

Still nothing.

“Okay.”

I looked around.

A woman carrying two shopping bags was approaching from the opposite direction.

She noticed the map.

“You trying to find the station?”

I looked up.

She was an adult, probably somewhere in her twenties, with short brown hair and a yellow cardigan over a white blouse. She looked like she'd been out shopping rather than heading anywhere in particular.

“Yeah.”

She glanced at the map.

“Which station?”

I showed her.

She leaned closer.

“Oh. That's a bit back.”

“Of course it is.”

She smiled.

“You came from that way?”

“Apparently.”

“Then you walked past it.”

I looked over my shoulder.

“How far?”

“Not very. Maybe five minutes.”

I sighed.

“Okay. Thanks.”

“No problem.”

She shifted the shopping bags in her hands.

“Just go back to the main road. There's a pharmacy on the corner. The station entrance is just after that.”

I nodded.

“Got it.”

She started walking again, then stopped.

“Actually, wait.”

I looked back.

“You're going the other direction.”

I stared at her.

She laughed.

“Sorry.”

“It's fine.”

She pointed behind me.

“That way.”

“Right.”

“Good luck.”

“Thanks.”

She continued down the road.

I waited until she was gone before looking at my map again.

“Fantastic.”

I turned around.

At least I knew where I was going now.

Mostly.

The station was larger than I expected.

It had several platforms, a broad entrance and enough people moving through it that I had to stop for a moment just to understand where I was supposed to go.

Announcements played over the speakers.

People talked over them.

A train arrived with a metallic rush, brakes squealing briefly before the doors opened.

A group of students hurried down the stairs.

Two office workers stood near a pillar drinking coffee from paper cups.

Someone was arguing with a ticket machine.

I wasn't sure how they had managed to start an argument with a machine, but somehow they had.

I bought my ticket after asking the clerk twice where I needed to go.

The clerk looked at me strangely.

I couldn't tell whether it was because of my voice, my appearance, or the fact that I looked completely lost.

Probably some combination of all three.

The train arrived a few minutes later.

I got on.

The carriage was crowded enough that I had to stand near the door.

I held the map against my chest.

As the train moved, the city slid past the windows.

Buildings gave way to smaller streets.

Smaller streets became wider roads.

Then trees.

Then more buildings.

The landscape changed gradually enough that I could watch it happen.

Ordinary houses with small gardens.

Apartment blocks packed closely together.

Convenience stores.

School buildings.

Telephone poles.

Narrow roads filled with bicycles.

Every so often the train passed a stretch of green where the city seemed to loosen its grip for a few minutes.

I found myself watching everything.

Sunlight on the windows.

Reflections of passengers.

The wires running alongside the railway.

Clouds moving across the sky.

Even the little scratches in the glass.

It was strange how beautiful ordinary things could look when you knew you'd lost the life that contained them.

I looked down at my hands.

For a moment, the old sadness returned.

I missed home.

I missed people I couldn't even call anymore.

I missed being able to complain about things that now seemed unbelievably small.

The thought sat there.

Then the train entered a tunnel.

The window became a dark mirror.

My new face appeared again.

I stared at it.

“Right.”

I looked away.

Not today.

I wasn't going to spend the entire day breaking apart.

The train emerged into sunlight.

I looked out again.

Kuoh was bigger than I'd expected.

The station alone gave me that impression.

There were more people than I had anticipated, more streets, more shops, more buildings and more traffic. It wasn't some tiny town where everyone knew everyone else.

It felt like an actual city.

A lively one.

I stepped out of the station and immediately realized I had no idea which direction to walk.

I unfolded the map.

A man nearly walked into me.

“Sorry.”

“Sorry.”

We both moved aside.

He was wearing a dark suit and carrying a briefcase, his black hair neatly combed back. He gave me a distracted nod and disappeared into the crowd before I could say anything else.

I looked at the map.

The streets around the station were dense.

I followed the route.

For ten minutes.

Then fifteen.

Then I realized I'd somehow crossed the same intersection twice.

I stopped.

“No.”

I looked behind me.

Then ahead.

Then at the map.

“This is the same street.”

A bicycle bell rang behind me.

I stepped aside.

A teenage girl rode past, her dark ponytail swinging behind her. She braked a few metres away and glanced back.

“You okay?”

“Yeah.”

She looked at the map in my hand.

“You looking for somewhere?”

“The academy.”

She nodded.

“Oh.”

She looked down the street.

“You went past the turn.”

I stared at the map.

“Again?”

She laughed.

“Yeah. Again.”

I looked at her.

She shrugged.

“It's easy to miss. The road bends.”

“Apparently I'm really good at this.”

“You're not.”

I stared at her.

She grinned.

“Sorry.”

I laughed despite myself.

“It's fine.”

She pointed farther down the road.

“Go back to that intersection. There's a bakery on the corner. Turn there and keep going.”

I looked where she was pointing.

“Then I'll get there?”

“Eventually.”

She said it casually, not as a joke.

I stared at her for a second.

“That's not very reassuring.”

She laughed.

“You'll be fine.”

Then she pushed off again.

“Thanks.”

She lifted one hand without turning around.

“Good luck.”

I watched her disappear into the crowd.

I looked at my map.

Maybe I needed a better map.

Or a better brain.

Possibly both.

Still, the city was starting to grow on me.

There was something different about the atmosphere here.

People were more expressive.

Not necessarily kinder.

Not necessarily friendlier.

Just... more.

A couple argued outside a café, neither particularly concerned about who could hear them. An elderly man sat nearby reading a newspaper and pretending not to listen. Two children ran past a shop window chasing each other while their mother shouted after them. A woman leaned out of an upstairs window to call something across the street.

A group of young adults passed in conversation, laughing loudly enough that people turned to look at them.

Even the way people dressed seemed slightly more striking.

There were plenty of ordinary clothes, but there was also an odd abundance of people who looked unusually polished, unusually attractive, or simply more physically exaggerated than I was used to seeing in everyday life. Tall people looked taller. Slender people looked almost unnaturally graceful. Women with naturally striking figures seemed to be everywhere, moving through the streets as though the city had somehow decided that ordinary proportions were merely a suggestion.

I caught myself staring once.

I looked away.

Okay.

So Kuoh was weird.

Not supernatural-weird.

Just...

Weird.

I kept walking.

By the time I reached the road leading toward the academy, the sun was higher.

The streets widened.

Buildings became more substantial.

There were more students around now.

Uniforms everywhere.

Some walked in groups.

Others rode bicycles.

A few hurried along with books pressed against their chests.

I passed a convenience store and stopped long enough to buy something to drink.

The cashier looked at me twice.

I couldn't blame him.

Long black-and-green hair.

Pale skin.

Slender frame.

A face that made it difficult to decide what I was supposed to be at a glance.

I paid and stepped outside.

A gust of wind caught my hair and sent half of it across my face.

I grabbed it.

“Seriously?”

A passing student laughed.

I looked over.

She immediately looked away, pretending she hadn't.

I shook my head and kept walking.

The closer I got to the academy, the stranger the city seemed.

Not frightening.

If anything, the opposite.

It felt almost too lively.

A group of students burst into laughter at the crossing.

Someone nearly dropped an entire stack of books and caught them against her chest at the last second.

Two boys were arguing over something that appeared to be completely pointless.

A teacher shouted after them.

A bicycle went past with a basket full of flowers.

A woman carrying groceries stopped in the middle of the pavement to talk to a friend, forcing half a dozen people to weave around them.

Nothing extraordinary was happening.

And yet everything seemed to have slightly more energy than it should.

I couldn't explain it.

I wasn't sure I wanted to.

For once, I was enjoying not knowing.

Then I saw the gates.

I stopped.

Kuoh Academy stood beyond them.

It was much larger than I'd imagined from the letter.

The grounds stretched far enough that I couldn't see the entire campus from the road. The main building rose beyond the entrance, surrounded by trees and carefully maintained paths. Other structures stood farther back, partly hidden behind greenery.

The architecture was elegant without looking old-fashioned.

Stone.

Glass.

Dark roofing.

Large windows catching the afternoon light.

Students moved through the grounds in groups, their voices carrying faintly toward the road.

The entire place looked expensive.

Not merely expensive in the way a nice school looked expensive.

Established.

Like it had been there long enough to develop its own gravity.

I stood there with the map still in my hand.

For the first time since waking up, I wasn't thinking about death.

I wasn't thinking about my old life.

I wasn't thinking about the mirror.

I was just looking.

Tomorrow I'd have to walk through those gates.

Tomorrow I'd take an entrance examination for a school I'd never heard of, in a city I'd only discovered that morning, while living in a body belonging to someone named Ira Lowe whose life I knew absolutely nothing about.

I looked down at the letter.

Then back at the academy.

I let out a slow breath.

“Well.”

A breeze moved through the trees.

Somewhere inside the campus, a bell rang.

Students began moving between buildings.

For a moment, sunlight caught the windows all at once, turning the upper floor bright enough that I had to squint.

I smiled despite myself.

This was insane.

Completely insane.

But it was also the first thing that had felt like a beginning.

I folded the map and put it away.

Tomorrow, I would take the exam.

Today, I had finally found somewhere to go.

Chapter 4 — Beyond
For a while, there was nothing.

Not darkness. Darkness would have been something—it would have implied a room waiting quietly in the shadows, or an overcast sky, or at least the faint, comforting sense of space stretching away into the dark.

There was none of that.

There was simply no sensation of being anywhere at all.

Then awareness returned.

I couldn't feel my body.

That was the first thing that drifted back into focus. There was no weight beneath me, no mattress or floor pressing against my back, no rhythm of air filling lungs. I couldn't feel my hands, my feet, or the temperature of the air. I couldn't even tell whether I was facing upward or downward, or if those directions even meant anything anymore.

I was conscious, and that was the only thing I possessed.

And then, without warning, the dark opened.

Stars filled everything.

For a long time, I couldn't do anything except stare.

They weren't the quiet, shimmering pinpricks I remembered seeing from suburban backyards. From Earth, stars had always seemed gentle—little flecks of diamond dusted across an ink-black dome, beautiful because they were too far away to hurt.

Out here, distance offered no shelter.

They burned with terrifying vitality. Some blazed blue-white and fierce, their light so dense and immediate it felt almost physical. Others smoldered deep ochre and crimson through curtains of interstellar gas that drifted across the expanse, vast sheets of glowing dust with neither beginning nor end. There were nurseries where newborn stars clustered so thickly that the black between them vanished into sheets of pearl, and beyond them, entire galaxies turned through the silence like glowing wheels.

The longer I drifted, the less the word sky made any sense.

There was no sky.

There was only an immensity that refused to stop opening.

Something drifted across my field of view.

At first, I thought it was a dark cloud cutting across the backdrop of distant galaxies. Then the light behind it reappeared, untouched, and the dizzying truth settled in: the void hadn't shifted at all.

I had.

Or something had moved me.

Direction had already lost its grip on me, dissolving into pure perspective.

Then the light ahead bent.

It was subtle at first—just a few background stars bowing out of place, their positions smearing across the dark like oil on water.

Then the distortion widened into a full, unbroken curve.

A ring of light flared into existence.

And in the center—

nothing.

I knew what it was.

A black hole.

I had seen pictures, artistic renderings, CGI models in science documentaries with soothing narrators explaining event horizons and photon spheres. But none of those sleek graphics prepared me for the visceral wrongness of the real thing.

Seeing it without an atmosphere or a computer monitor between us was terrifying.

The blackness at its core wasn't a shadow. It was an absolute cancellation. Starlight striking the outer boundary simply died, while the surrounding field was dragged along its edge in warped, blinding arcs. The accretion disk twisted the logic of sight: the far edge arched up over the dark center, glowing like an impossible halo, while the underside wrapped beneath it. Light that should have traveled straight had been forced into circles, bent by a mass so heavy the fabric of reality seemed to sag beneath it.

It didn't look like a physical object.

It looked like a hole torn cleanly out of the universe.

And as I drifted farther, I realized it was only one of many.

Beyond it lay depths that made the singularity look like an afterthought. Stars that had seemed colossal shrank into embers. Galaxies blurred into pale smudges. Structures so vast I lacked the language to describe them rose from the dark, hung suspended, and then dwindled into specks against whatever lay further out.

The universe wasn't growing.

I was just finally far enough away to realize how small my imagination had always been.

It should have broken me.

Instead, a strange, hollow wonder took over.

I had spent seventeen years looking up at the sky, convinced I understood what space meant.

I didn't know anything at all.

Then the framework collapsed.

There was no sound, no flash, no threshold to mark where one reality ended and the next began.

The rules that kept things apart simply stopped working.

A shape unfolded in front of me.

I called it a shape only because my mind had nothing else to reach for. Its outer surface folded smoothly inward and somehow emerged behind itself. Another structure intersected it without a collision, sliding through solid faces without leaving a tear. A line extended away from me and returned from the opposite direction, arriving behind my perspective without ever turning a corner.

I tried tracking a single edge just to anchor myself.

I couldn't.

Every time I thought I had grasped where it led, the planes rearranged themselves.

Inside became outside.

Distant points became near.

A boundary that should have closed something off ended up holding the empty space around it. I couldn't tell if the geometry was folding in front of me, or if my own mind was being bent to fit an impossible angle.

Then everything compressed.

Not by shrinking.

Things simply moved closer together while keeping their scale. Distances squeezed into zero space, forcing near and far into the exact same coordinates. For a breathless moment, there was nowhere left to exist because everywhere was happening at once.

Then the tension snapped.

The impossible forms drifted apart, loosening their grip, and faded into the dark.

I kept moving.

How long it lasted, I couldn't say.

Time eventually became impossible to hold onto.

At the beginning, I tried counting. Seconds, minutes, hours—anything to create a rhythm. But the numbers lost their weight. Hours blurred into stretches that felt like decades. I remember waiting. I remember the heavy, hollow ache of being entirely alone. I remember the creeping numbness that comes when you realize there is nothing left to react to.

Yet if someone had demanded an accounting of those years, I wouldn't have had a single memory to offer.

There was no yesterday.

No morning.

No evening.

No markers on a wall.

Only an endless stretch of before and after, pulled so thin that the difference evaporated completely.

I was there for lifetimes.

Or maybe a few seconds.

Eventually, even the passage of time stopped registering.

Then the light went out.

The blackness that followed was distinct from everything that had preceded it.

There was nothing waiting behind it. No dormant stars hiding in the distance. No nebular dust, no outlines, no horizon.

Just absence.

It wasn't a peaceful dark. It pressed against me, thick and suffocating.

I tried to breathe, forgetting that I had no chest to expand. There was no ribcage to tighten, no skin for cold to prickle, no pulse to hammer against my temples.

Yet the panic came anyway.

I wanted out.

Then, a thread of light caught my eye.

It started faint, a thin ribbon of pale blue drifting in the far distance. Then violet bled into it, followed by jade, and then an incandescent, liquid gold. The colors wove into currents, broad rivers of radiance coursing through the void as if an entire hidden ocean had suddenly decided to ignite.

It was breathtaking.

After so much emptiness, I wanted nothing more than to drift into it and stay there.

The currents began to pick up speed.

I didn't accelerate—I had no body to propel. But the space between us simply vanished. The ribbons lengthened, smearing into long streaks that erased the line between movement and illumination.

Then speed ceased to be an adequate word.

I was being carried somewhere.

Far beyond light. Far beyond anything humanity had ever measured or named.

And then, looking back across the distance, I saw it.

A solitary sphere.

Pale, blue-white, and impossibly fragile.

It took a few heartbeats for understanding to catch up.

The observable universe.

I stared back at it, transfixed.

It was so small.

Everything I had ever known was tucked inside that little marble.

Earth.

The sun.

Every star humans had ever mapped or written songs about.

Every street I had walked down, my high school, my home.

My mother.

Daniel.

Every single life, memory, and piece of history had played out inside that tiny, glowing bubble.

And I was slipping away from it.

I tried to reach out. I tried to arrest the drift, to anchor myself to anything.

Nothing answered.

The sphere shrank, dwindling into a solitary point of light in an ocean of unfamiliar dark.

The terror hit me then—sharp, raw, and desperate.

There was no heart to race in my chest. No throat to close up, no lungs to hitch, no hands to claw at the void.

And yet I was terrified.

The contradiction made it worse. How could terror exist when there was nothing left of me to be afraid?

I didn't know. I only knew that I wanted to go back.

The speck vanished.

Ahead, another boundary rose to meet me.

It didn't glow. It carried no discernible form or geometry. It possessed only an absolute, ancient presence, standing like a wall erected before the beginning of things.

I drew closer.

It felt heavy—not with mass, but with the quiet inevitability of something that had always existed and never needed to justify itself.

I met the edge.

For a fractured instant, everything hummed.

Space, time, identity, every memory of who I was and where I had been—all of it tangled together into a single, blinding point of tension.

Then—

BOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOM—

The universe shattered into light.

It wasn't a sound, but it struck harder than any thunderclap could have. Sensation overloaded entirely, burning out thought, sight, and self.

Then, silence.

And then—

the smell of damp earth.

Cold air.

The rough prickle of grass.

My eyes snapped open.

Above me, resting against the dark, was a moon.

Full. Pale. Familiar.

I was lying on a grassy hill next to an empty road.

For a long time, I stayed completely still, listening.

Crickets stirred in the tall grass nearby. Farther off, deep in a line of trees, an owl called into the evening. A chill breeze moved across the slope, bending the blades of grass until they brushed against my bare arms.

A car drove past along the asphalt below.

Its headlights washed over the slope, caught the gravel shoulder for a few seconds, and disappeared around a bend.

I watched the red taillights fade until the night reclaimed the asphalt.

The sheer normality of it made my head spin.

After where I had been, the hill felt claustrophobic. The road looked toy-like. The moon looked like a prop hung on a wire, entirely too close to the ground. The whole world felt as though it had been shrunk down to fit inside a box.

I shut my eyes.

The dark behind my lids hitched.

I snapped them open.

The moon was still there, silver and calm.

I closed them again.

There it was. For a microsecond, the blackness behind my eyes twisted, as if the reality in front of me had failed to render a frame. Not a picture, not a lingering afterimage. Just a tiny tear in the fabric of things.

I opened my eyes. Nothing.

I shut them.

It happened again.

And again.

Each time, the stutter grew fainter, smoothing out until the dark was just dark again.

Slowly, I pushed myself up.

That was when the first true wrongness hit.

My body.

I lifted a hand, turning it under the moonlight.

It was a hand. Five fingers, pale skin, neatly trimmed nails. It flexed when I wanted it to flex.

That should have been reassuring.

It wasn't.

The motion had been too fluid, executing a fraction of a heartbeat before I had fully finished willing it. It was like wearing gloves tailored so precisely they felt like a second skin, yet entirely alien beneath the surface.

I stood up.

My weight shifted, my balance correcting itself instantly with an effortless, predatory grace that wasn't mine.

I took one step, then another.

The body moved with quiet confidence, adjusting to the slope of the hill faster than my thoughts could track.

I stopped.

My gaze snapped to the treeline.

Then down the road to the drainage ditch.

Then to the blind corner where the road curved toward a cluster of distant buildings.

I stood frozen on the grass, my pulse steady, my breathing slow.

Why did I just check those?

I hadn't thought about escape routes or cover. The assessment had simply occurred, clean and instinctive, before I had even realized I was looking.

I forced myself to start walking again.

With every yard, the disconnect grew quieter, settling into the muscle and bone until the mechanics felt seamless. Not familiar. Never familiar. Just natural.

I drew a breath through my teeth and tried to speak.

“Hello?”

The sound broke the night, and I froze.

That wasn't my voice.

It was softer. A higher pitch, smooth and edged with a cadence I didn't recognize.

My throat worked, swallowing hard.

“Hello?” I tried again.

The tone modulated slightly, warming, adjusting to the shape of the mouth.

“Okay,” I whispered.

The word came out smoother this time, settling into a distinct, foreign register, as if the vocal cords were remembering how to function after a long silence.

I stared down at the asphalt, my chest tightening.

“What the hell...?”

Hearing those syllables carried by someone else's voice made my stomach drop.

I had to get off the road. I needed four walls, a roof, anywhere private where I could sit down and pull my mind back together.

I followed the road until it reached a three-story residential building. The outer gate sat unlatched, swinging slightly on its hinge, and the front door yielded with a quiet click when I turned the handle.

Inside, the air was still and cool.

An apartment.

It was dark, lit only by the amber glow of a streetlamp cutting through the sheer curtains.

It was empty, but it wasn't abandoned.

A ceramic mug sat near the sink with a thin ring dried at the bottom. A jacket hung over the back of a kitchen chair. A low shelf held paperbacks with creased spines, and small, everyday knick-knacks sat on the side table with the casual disarray of a life temporarily stepped away from.

Someone lived here.

I walked softly down the narrow hall, my socks making almost no sound against the wood.

There were no answers resting on the counter. No driver's license left out, no mail stacked with a name and an address, no framed family photos smiling from the wall. Just the quiet, lingering imprint of an interrupted routine.

At the end of the short corridor, I reached the bathroom.

The door stood open.

A tall mirror hung above the sink, catching the faint, bluish ambient light from the high window.

I stopped.

My mind locked up, refusing for several long seconds to assemble the visual data in front of me.

The figure in the glass looked back.

It stood exactly where I stood. It wore the clothes I was wearing. Its chest rose and fell in time with my own breath.

It wasn't Jonah.

I stared into the glass.

The unfamiliar, arresting eyes stared back from beneath strands of hair that weren't mine, framing a face I had never seen before in my life.

My jaw went slack.

“What the fuck?”
