documents.body:
Chapter 3 — Maybe Tomorrow
I woke up before my alarm.

Again.

For a few seconds, I just lay there.

The ceiling was still the ceiling.

Same pale paint.

Same thin crack running from the corner toward the light fixture.

I had been meaning to fix that.

For months.

I reached for my phone.

6:11.

My alarm was set for 6:30.

Nineteen minutes.

I could go back to sleep.

I probably should.

Instead, I sat up.

For some reason, that felt like an accomplishment.

Not a big one.

Just enough to make me feel like I'd done something right.

I stood.

My feet hit the cold floor.

I walked to the mirror.

My hair was a mess.

My eyes looked tired.

I stared at myself.

"Ugly."

I waited.

"...Not ugly."

Another pause.

"Average."

I frowned.

Why did I keep doing that?

Maybe because average was such a strange word.

It wasn't an insult.

It wasn't a compliment.

It just meant normal.

And I hated how much I hated being normal.

I left the room.

Mom was already in the kitchen.

She looked over when I walked in.

"You woke up early."

"I guess."

She glanced at the clock.

"You have school in an hour."

"I know."

"So why are you standing there?"

I looked around the kitchen.

"...I don't know."

She shook her head.

There was a plate on the table.

I sat down.

She put a cup beside it.

"Eat."

"I was going to."

"You say that every morning."

"And every morning I eventually eat."

"After I tell you."

"Still counts."

She gave me a look.

I smiled.

She tried not to.

Didn't quite manage it.

For a moment, everything was normal.

Just breakfast.

Just Mom.

Just another morning.

Then she said:

"You know, you used to wake up at five."

I stopped.

"What?"

"When you were little."

"No, I didn't."

"You did."

"Why?"

She shrugged.

"You wanted to watch the sunrise."

I smiled.

"That's embarrassing."

"You were six."

"Still embarrassing."

"You used to drag your blanket into the living room and sit by the window."

I stared at her.

"I don't remember that."

"I do."

She went back to what she was doing.

I smiled again.

I liked that.

There were apparently versions of me that existed in other people's memories.

Versions I'd forgotten.

Six-year-old Jonah.

Sitting by a window before sunrise because he wanted to see something.

I wondered what happened to that kid.

Mom handed me my lunch.

"Don't forget this."

I looked at the bag.

"Oh."

She raised an eyebrow.

"Thanks."

"You're welcome, Jonah Laurence."

The full name.

That meant I was supposed to be paying attention.

I took the bag.

"See you later."

"Don't be late."

"I won't."

I left.

The morning was ordinary.

Cars.

People.

A dog barking behind a fence.

Someone arguing about a parking space.

A bus groaning its way down the road.

Nothing strange.

Nothing dramatic.

Nothing worth remembering.

I liked mornings like this.

Because nobody was paying attention to me.

And for once, I didn't mind.

Daniel was waiting near the corner.

The second he saw me, he raised one hand.

"Finally!"

"I'm early."

"You're four minutes late."

"Then you're four minutes early."

He stared at me.

"That's not how time works."

"It is if I'm the one who's late."

"That doesn't even make sense."

"Sounds like a you problem."

He laughed.

We started walking.

A few seconds passed.

Then he looked at me.

"So."

"So?"

"The assignment."

I looked at him.

He looked at me.

Neither of us said anything.

Then we both started laughing.

"You're useless," he said.

"You asked me knowing the answer."

"I was hoping you'd become disciplined overnight."

I shrugged.

"I woke up before my alarm."

Daniel stopped walking.

"What?"

"Yeah."

He looked genuinely concerned.

"Who are you?"

"Shut up."

"I'm serious."

"I just woke up early."

"That's exactly what a replacement would say."

I shoved his shoulder.

He laughed.

I laughed too.

And just like that, the morning became easier.

School was normal.

Mostly.

Teachers talked.

Students complained.

Pens disappeared.

Someone got yelled at for talking.

Daniel nearly made me laugh in class.

I nearly got caught.

Then break came.

We sat behind the science block where the concrete wall blocked most of the noise.

The sun had warmed the pavement.

Daniel was telling me a story.

A stupid story.

Which meant it was probably true.

"...and then she tells me I'm supposed to apologize."

"You probably did something."

"I didn't."

"You definitely did."

"I did not."

"What did you say?"

He hesitated.

"That's not important."

I laughed.

"Then you did something."

"Okay, technically—"

"Exactly."

He threw a bottle cap at me.

I caught it.

"You're annoying."

"You're the one who started it."

"That's debatable."

"No, it isn't."

We laughed again.

For a while, neither of us cared about anything.

Eventually the conversation drifted.

Money.

School.

The future.

Daniel wanted to be rich.

"How rich?"

"Rich."

"That's not a number."

"Enough."

"Enough for what?"

"Everything."

I shook my head.

"That's not a plan."

"Sure it is."

He looked at me.

"What about you?"

"What?"

"What do you want?"

I opened my mouth.

A joke came first.

I almost said it.

Instead, I shrugged.

"I don't know."

Daniel frowned.

"You're seventeen."

"So?"

"You're not supposed to know."

I smiled.

"Maybe."

He nudged my shoulder.

"You'll figure it out."

Simple.

He said it like it was obvious.

I didn't answer.

But I remembered it.

The cyberbullying started again after lunch.

I knew before I even opened my phone.

That little hesitation.

That instinctive feeling that something unpleasant was waiting behind the screen.

I opened the app.

One post.

Then another.

A screenshot of something I'd said weeks ago.

A caption.

A reply.

Another reply.

I scrolled.

More.

Some of it was stupid.

Some of it was exaggerated.

Some of it wasn't even true.

That should have made it easier.

It didn't.

I kept reading.

Then I read the comments again.

Why?

I didn't know.

Maybe I was looking for the point where it stopped hurting.

It didn't.

I locked my phone.

Put it face-down.

Looked at the board.

The teacher was talking.

I listened.

For maybe ten seconds.

My phone buzzed.

I ignored it.

Another buzz.

I looked at it.

Don't.

I picked it up.

More messages.

My face felt hot.

I locked it again.

Why do I care?

Because everyone else cared.

Or I thought they did.

That was the problem.

I didn't actually know what anyone thought.

I knew what I imagined they thought.

Sometimes those felt exactly the same.

I put my phone away.

They're right.

I stared at the board.

No, they're not.

A second passed.

Why do I care?

Because everyone else cares.

Do they?

Doesn't matter.

I looked around the classroom.

Nobody was looking at me.

At least...

I didn't think they were.

A guy two seats ahead laughed.

My brain immediately supplied an explanation.

He's laughing about you.

I caught myself.

You don't know that.

I watched him for another second.

He was talking to his friend.

Probably something completely unrelated.

I looked away.

That bothered me.

Not because I was necessarily wrong.

Because I had no idea whether I was right.

And I'd already decided.

After class, someone caught up with me.

"Jonah."

I turned.

She held out a notebook.

"You left this."

I took it.

"Oh."

"You were kind of quiet earlier."

"I'm fine."

She hesitated.

"You sure?"

Something inside me tightened.

I hated that question.

Not because it was bad.

Because I didn't know how to answer it.

"Yeah."

She looked at me.

I looked away.

Then I said:

"You don't have to do that."

"Do what?"

"Feel sorry for me."

She blinked.

"I wasn't."

"Whatever."

I walked away.

My steps felt too fast.

I made it around the corner.

Stopped.

Looked back.

She was still standing there.

She didn't look angry.

She looked confused.

Genuinely confused.

My stomach sank.

Oh.

I knew what I'd done.

She'd noticed I wasn't doing well.

That's it.

She hadn't insulted me.

She hadn't mocked me.

She hadn't even said anything particularly personal.

She'd just...

noticed.

And I'd decided what she meant before I actually knew.

Again.

I rubbed my face.

I'm an asshole.

Then another thought came.

No.

You're embarrassed.

I frowned.

That's not an excuse.

I stood there for a few seconds.

That was the annoying thing about self-awareness.

Sometimes you could watch yourself making a mistake in real time.

And still make it.

Maybe that was what discipline actually meant.

Not waking up early.

Not making schedules.

Not pretending you suddenly had your entire life under control.

Maybe it meant being able to stop yourself.

Think.

Then act.

I liked that idea.

A lot.

Because if that was true...

then maybe I could actually change.

By the time school ended, I felt better.

Not happy.

Not miserable.

Just...

bummed out.

There was a difference.

I could still laugh.

I could still talk.

I could still look forward to things.

I just had this annoying weight sitting somewhere behind my ribs.

Seventeen.

That number kept coming back.

Seventeen.

Still young.

But somehow already late.

Everyone kept saying I had time.

Of course I had time.

But how much of it had I already wasted?

Childhood was gone.

I couldn't get it back.

Years I'd spent doing stupid things.

Hours I'd spent scrolling.

Days I'd wasted.

Opportunities I'd ignored.

What if I'd started earlier?

What if I'd been more disciplined?

What if I'd actually taken myself seriously?

Maybe I'd be better by now.

Maybe I'd be smarter.

More confident.

More talented.

More—

I stopped myself.

That was the trap.

I didn't need to become some extraordinary person.

I just wanted to become better.

That should have been enough.

But there was a part of me that wanted more.

A part that hated the idea of being average.

I knew talent mattered.

Of course it did.

Some people were simply better at things.

Some people learned faster.

Some people were naturally attractive.

Some people were naturally confident.

Some people could walk into a room and own it without even trying.

That was life.

I understood that.

I just didn't like it.

Because if talent wasn't enough...

then what was?

Work.

Discipline.

Consistency.

Control.

Those words felt better.

They made the future feel less random.

I could make a plan.

Wake up earlier.

Exercise.

Study properly.

Read more.

Learn something useful.

Use my phone less.

Talk to people more.

Sleep properly.

Stop procrastinating.

Stop reacting.

Actually...

Maybe I could write all of it down.

A real schedule.

Something I'd actually follow.

I felt myself getting excited.

Not because I believed I'd become perfect.

Just because—

I could change.

That thought hit differently.

I could actually change.

Maybe I wasn't late.

Maybe I just hadn't started.

Then another thought slipped in.

If I control everything I can control...

I paused.

That sounded reasonable.

...then eventually things have to go right.

I knew that wasn't entirely true.

Obviously.

Life didn't work like that.

But it was close enough to something true that I wanted to believe it.

If I couldn't control other people, I could control myself.

If I couldn't control the past, I could control tomorrow.

If I couldn't control whether people liked me, I could control whether I respected myself.

That was enough.

It had to be.

I started walking again.

Tomorrow.

I'd start tomorrow.

Daniel caught up with me near the school gate.

"You going home?"

"Yeah."

"Same."

We walked together.

For a while, neither of us said anything.

Then Daniel looked at me.

"You know what?"

"What?"

"You're actually less annoying when you're not thinking so hard."

I laughed.

"That's your nicest insult yet."

"I'm serious."

"Thanks?"

He smiled.

Then he pointed at me.

"Don't forget the assignment."

"I won't."

"You will."

"I won't."

"You absolutely will."

"Watch me."

He started walking backward.

"I know you, Laurence."

I smiled.

"Go home."

He turned around.

I watched him disappear down the street.

For some reason, I stayed there.

Just for a moment.

Then I went home.

The evening was quiet.

I ate.

I did some homework.

Not much.

I spent too long on my phone.

Ironically.

Then I opened my notes app.

I typed:

Things I need to fix.

I stared at it.

Then started listing things.

Wake up earlier.

Exercise.

Study.

Read.

Less phone.

More social.

Better sleep.

Stop reacting emotionally.

Actually finish things.

Learn something useful.

Figure out what I want.

I stared at the list.

It was ridiculous.

It was ambitious.

It was probably unrealistic.

I smiled anyway.

Maybe that was okay.

Maybe I didn't have to know how everything would work.

Maybe I just had to start.

Tomorrow.

I put my phone down.

A few minutes later, it buzzed.

I picked it up.

Unknown number.

I opened the message.

You looked happy today.

My smile disappeared.

Another message appeared.

Enjoy it while you can.

I stared at the screen.

My chest tightened.

I blocked the number.

Then I sat there.

Waiting.

Nothing happened.

No new message.

No call.

Nothing.

I put the phone down.

Ignore it.

That was the sensible thing.

So I did.

For about thirty seconds.

Then I picked it up again.

Nothing.

I locked it.

Put it away.

I wasn't going to let some anonymous idiot ruin my evening.

I had plans.

Tomorrow.

I'd start tomorrow.

I went to bed later than I should have.

I stared at the ceiling.

The crack was still there.

Same as this morning.

Same as yesterday.

Same as—

I stopped.

The previous night.

The thing in my room.

The darkness.

The breathing.

The voice.

I remembered it.

My skin prickled.

Maybe it had been a nightmare.

Probably.

Stress.

Too much screen time.

Whatever.

My brain had probably just...

done something weird.

That happened.

I turned onto my side.

Tomorrow was Thursday.

School.

Daniel.

Maybe I'd apologize to that girl.

Maybe.

I'd start the schedule.

I'd actually stick to it this time.

I'd get better.

Not perfect.

Just better.

That was enough.

Wasn't it?

I closed my eyes.

And slept.

The next afternoon, I was going home.

I remember that.

I remember the sun.

I remember the pavement.

I remember thinking about the list on my phone.

I remember thinking I should probably add don't procrastinate to it.

Then someone slammed into my shoulder.

Hard.

"What the—"

My hand went empty.

I looked down.

Nothing.

I looked ahead.

The guy was already running.

My phone was in his hand.

For half a second, I just stood there.

Then my brain caught up.

"HEY!"

He kept running.

"HEY! GIVE THAT BACK!"

I took off.

My shoes hammered the pavement.

SMACK! SMACK! SMACK!

He was fast.

Not impossibly fast.

Just fast enough.

"STOP!"

He didn't.

I pushed harder.

My phone.

That was all I cared about.

My phone.

Everything was on that thing.

Pictures.

Messages.

Notes.

Accounts.

My stupid schedule.

The list.

Tomorrow.

I could see the blue case.

Mine.

I was gaining on him.

Maybe.

No.

Definitely.

"GIVE IT BACK!"

He looked over his shoulder.

That was when I knew I was catching him.

Five meters.

Maybe six.

My lungs burned.

My heart hammered against my ribs.

THUD. THUD. THUD.

I pushed harder.

Then—

VRRROOOOOOOOOOOOM—

Something roared somewhere beside me.

I barely noticed.

The thief was still ahead.

I kept running.

THUD. THUD. THUD.

My heartbeat.

My shoes.

My breath.

Everything narrowing.

Thief.

Phone.

Run.

Then rain touched my cheek.

One drop.

Tap.

Another.

Tap.

I glanced upward.

The sky had changed.

Clouds had swallowed the afternoon.

That was weird.

It had been clear.

Hadn't it?

Then—

SHHHHHHHHHHHHHHH.

Rain poured down.

"What the hell?!"

It didn't matter.

The thief was still ahead.

I ran.

The road seemed longer now.

Maybe it was the rain.

Maybe I'd taken a wrong turn.

I couldn't tell.

There.

The thief.

Still running.

Still carrying my phone.

"COME BACK!"

My voice cracked.

I pushed harder.

SMACK! SMACK! SMACK!

Then something enormous moved through the edge of my vision.

Black.

Tall.

Fast.

I didn't look.

I couldn't.

The thief was right there.

Eight meters.

Seven.

Six.

I reached.

"HEY!"

The engine behind me grew louder.

Not louder.

Closer.

VRRROOOOOOOOOOOOOOMMMMM—

The pavement trembled beneath my shoes.

My teeth clicked together.

I barely registered it.

The thief was getting away.

Five meters.

Four.

I stretched my hand out.

"GOT YOU—!"

A shadow swallowed the road.

The rain around me exploded sideways.

WHOOOOOOOOM!

Wind slammed into my body.

I stumbled.

"What—"

The sound behind me changed.

A metallic shriek.

A monstrous grinding roar.

KRRRRRRRRRRRRRRAAAAAAAAAAAAAA—

I turned.

Just a little.

Just enough.

And finally saw it.

Black metal.

Rain.

Headlights.

A wall.

No.

Not a wall.

A vehicle.

Maybe.

My brain couldn't make sense of the size.

It towered over the street.

The thing seemed to stretch backward into the rain forever.

The road looked tiny beneath it.

Wrong.

Everything about it was wrong.

I stared.

My mouth opened.

"What the fuck—?!"

The headlights hit me.

WHITE.

My body understood before my brain did.

MOVE.

I tried.

My foot slipped.

The world lurched.

BOOOOOOOOOOOOOOM!

Pain.

Noise.

White.

I didn't know which way was up.

Something hit me.

Then something else.

BANG!

The road flashed beneath me.

Sky.

Road.

Sky.

Rain.

Black.

White.

CRACK!

I couldn't breathe.

I tried.

Nothing.

My ears were screaming.

No—

Not screaming.

Everything was screaming.

SKRRRRRRRRRRRRRRR—

I couldn't feel my legs.

I couldn't feel one of my hands.

I tried to move.

Nothing.

My thoughts were everywhere.

Too fast.

Then too slow.

Mom.

The kitchen.

A cup on the table.

Eat.

Daniel.

You're four minutes late.

No.

Four minutes early.

Whatever.

I almost smiled.

Almost.

Then the ceiling.

That stupid crack.

The mirror.

Average.

Why did I say that?

Why did I always—

The sunlight through the living-room window.

A blanket dragging across the floor.

Six.

I was six.

Wasn't I?

Mom remembered.

I didn't.

I tried to hold onto the image.

A window.

Orange light.

Warm.

Then it was gone.

The classroom came back.

The board.

The phone buzzing.

The comments.

They're right.

No.

They're not.

Someone laughing.

Someone—

The girl.

The notebook.

Her face.

You sure?

My stomach dropped.

I hadn't even—

I'm sorry.

I tried to say it.

Nothing.

My mouth wouldn't—

The road.

The thief.

My phone.

Where was my phone?

That stupid blue case.

I had been chasing—

Why?

Right.

Because it was mine.

My list.

The notes app.

I hadn't finished it.

There was something missing.

Something I'd meant to add.

What was it?

I tried to remember.

My thoughts slipped.

Wake up early.

Already did.

Exercise.

Tomorrow.

Study.

Tomorrow.

Read.

Tomorrow.

Everything was tomorrow.

The word floated there.

Tomorrow.

Tomorrow.

Tomorrow.

Daniel.

School.

Mom.

The assignment.

I still hadn't—

Tomorrow.

My chest tightened.

No.

I had time.

I did.

I was seventeen.

Seventeen wasn't old.

It wasn't.

I hadn't—

I hadn't even started.

The rain fell across my face.

For a second, it didn't feel cold.

Just quiet.

Tap.

A drop landed on my cheek.

Tap.

Another.

The sound seemed very far away.

I thought about Mom again.

Not anything important.

Not some final speech.

Just breakfast.

Her looking at me.

That little almost-smile.

"You're welcome, Jonah Laurence."

I wanted to hear it again.

I wanted—

My thoughts broke apart.

Daniel.

The window.

The list.

The girl.

The phone.

Mom.

The sunrise.

All of them blurred together.

I couldn't tell which memory came first.

I couldn't tell what I was trying to remember.

I only knew I didn't want to forget.

My vision dimmed.

The rain became white lines.

Then grey.

Then nothing I could understand.

I tried to move my hand.

Nothing.

I tried again.

Nothing.

And somewhere inside all that noise, one thought remained.

Not profound.

Not brave.

Not even complete.

Just something I'd believed so easily that I'd never bothered to question it.

Tomorrow.

I waited for the rest of the thought.

It didn't come.

My mind reached for it.

Nothing.

Then, somehow—

...I'll do better.

A tiny thought.

Almost stupid.

Almost hopeful.

I believed it.

Even then.

I believed there would be a tomorrow.

Then—

nothing.

I woke up before my alarm.

Not by much.

My phone said 6:17.

My alarm was set for 6:30.

I stared at the ceiling for a few seconds, trying to remember why I was awake.

Then I remembered.

I looked toward my bedroom door.

It was closed.

I didn't move.

Nothing happened.

After a while, I let out the breath I'd apparently been holding.

“Okay.”

My voice sounded stupidly quiet.

I reached for my phone.

No messages.

No notifications.

Nothing.

I checked anyway.

Then I checked again.

I didn't know what I expected to find.

Maybe a message from whoever had been sending those things last night.

Maybe some explanation.

Maybe proof that I hadn't imagined the whole thing.

There was nothing.

I put the phone against my chest and stared at the ceiling again.

There was a thin crack running across it, just above where I slept. I'd noticed it months ago. It wasn't getting bigger or anything. It was just there.

I'd spent enough mornings looking at it that I could almost trace the whole thing from memory.

My hair was probably a mess.

Actually, definitely a mess.

I ran a hand through it and felt a few strands sticking out in completely different directions.

Great.

I got out of bed.

My room looked exactly how I'd left it.

School uniform hanging off the back of my chair.

Bag on the floor.

Two textbooks underneath my desk.

One sock beside the bed.

The other sock had disappeared sometime during the week.

I had accepted that I would never see it again.

I picked up my uniform and got dressed.

In the mirror, I looked tired.

Not dramatically tired.

Just seventeen.

Messy hair. Slightly puffy eyes. Nothing particularly memorable about my face unless someone was already looking at me.

I leaned closer to the mirror.

“Ugly.”

I paused.

“Not ugly.”

Another pause.

“Average.”

That sounded fair.

I fixed my hair anyway.

My mother was already in the kitchen.

She was drinking tea while looking at her phone.

“Morning.”

“Morning.”

“You're going to school?”

I looked at her.

“Yes.”

“I mean, are you ready?”

“Obviously.”

She nodded and went back to her phone.

That was pretty much breakfast.

I opened the cupboard, found bread, and made myself something to eat.

The kitchen was small enough that two people could make it feel crowded without actually getting in each other's way.

The refrigerator made a low humming noise.

A tap somewhere near the sink dripped every few seconds.

Outside, somebody was already arguing with somebody else.

Normal morning.

I liked mornings like this.

Because nobody was paying attention to me.

I finished eating, grabbed my bag, and left.

The air outside was already warm.

Our street was busy in the way it always was in the morning. People heading somewhere. Cars squeezing past each other. Shops opening. Someone sweeping dirt from directly in front of a shop and somehow putting half of it back onto the road.

I walked with my hands in my pockets.

For the first few minutes, I didn't think about anything.

Then my phone buzzed.

I stopped.

It was Daniel.

Daniel: where are you

I replied.

Me: outside

Three seconds later:

Daniel: revolutionary answer

I smiled.

Me: shut up

Daniel: hurry up idiot

I put my phone away.

Daniel was waiting near the corner when I got there.

He was around my height, dark-skinned, with short hair and his school shirt already looking like he'd been wearing it for three hours instead of twenty minutes.

He looked at me.

Then at my hair.

Then back at me.

“What?”

“You look like you fought a pillow.”

“I won.”

“Clearly.”

I pushed him.

He laughed.

We started walking.

Daniel could talk about absolutely nothing for an impressive amount of time.

This morning it was football.

Then a teacher.

Then some video he'd seen.

Then football again.

I mostly listened.

Occasionally I disagreed just to annoy him.

“You're wrong.”

“I haven't even finished.”

“Still wrong.”

“You don't even know what I'm saying.”

“I know enough.”

“That doesn't even make sense.”

“It doesn't have to.”

He shook his head.

“You're actually annoying.”

“Thank you.”

School was school.

The gate was crowded.

Students were everywhere, uniforms mixing together until everybody looked like part of the same moving mass.

I hated that part.

Not because I hated people.

I just hated having to squeeze through them while pretending I wasn't trying to squeeze through them.

Inside, the classroom was already getting loud.

Chairs scraped against the floor.

Someone was laughing at the back.

A fan turned slowly above us, making a clicking sound every few rotations.

I sat down.

Daniel dropped into the seat beside me.

“Did you do the assignment?”

I looked at him.

“No.”

He looked relieved.

“Good.”

“You didn't either?”

“No.”

“Why are you relieved?”

“I thought you were going to make me feel bad.”

“That would've required me doing it.”

“Exactly.”

We laughed.

For a few minutes, everything was normal.

Actually normal.

No strange noises.

No anonymous messages.

No staring at the ceiling at three in the morning wondering whether I was awake.

Just school.

And honestly?

I preferred it that way.

Maya came over before the teacher arrived.

She had her hair tied back neatly and carried two notebooks against her chest.

“You people didn't do the assignment?”

Daniel immediately pointed at me.

“He didn't.”

“Traitor.”

“You're the one who said you didn't do it.”

Maya looked at both of us.

“You're both idiots.”

“That's fair,” I said.

She smiled and went back to her seat.

That was it.

Nothing dramatic.

Sometimes people were just people.

I think I'd forgotten that lately.

By break time, I'd almost stopped thinking about the night before.

Almost.

Daniel had convinced us to go behind the science block because apparently that was where people went when they wanted to waste ten minutes.

There wasn't anything particularly interesting there.

Just a concrete wall, some grass, a few old pipes and enough shade to make it cooler than the main courtyard.

We sat around talking.

Someone started telling a story about a teacher.

Another person interrupted halfway through.

Then everybody started arguing about what had actually happened.

I laughed so hard at one point that I nearly choked.

Daniel slapped my back.

“You good?”

I waved him off, still coughing.

“Yeah. Your stupid story just tried to kill me.”

“That's not my fault.”

“You're literally the one who told it.”

“Yeah, but you didn't have to laugh that hard.”

I gave him a look.

He shrugged.

“That's on you.”

I laughed again.

For those few minutes, I forgot about my phone.

That was probably the best part.

Then I checked it.

I had three notifications.

One was from a group chat.

The other two were screenshots.

I opened the first.

Someone had posted something about me.

Nothing technically new.

Someone had taken something I'd said, changed the wording, and made it sound worse.

The comments underneath were worse.

Some people believed it.

Some people didn't.

A few people were clearly just enjoying themselves.

I stared at the screen.

Daniel noticed.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

He leaned over.

I turned the phone away.

“Seriously?”

“Yeah.”

He didn't push.

That was one thing I liked about him.

He could be annoying as hell, but sometimes he knew when to leave something alone.

I locked my phone.

For the rest of lunch, I talked.

I laughed.

I even forgot about it again.

Then somebody across the courtyard looked at me.

I looked away first.

I hated that I did that.

The strange thing about rumors was that you never knew exactly how far they'd travelled.

You'd hear one version.

Then another.

Then somebody would mention something completely different.

Sometimes I'd wonder what people actually believed.

Sometimes I'd wonder what they were saying when I wasn't there.

That was the part I hated most.

Not knowing.

If somebody hated me to my face, at least I knew where I stood.

When I got home that afternoon, I checked my phone again.

Nothing new.

I threw it onto my bed.

Five minutes later, I picked it back up.

Still nothing.

I put it down again.

Then picked it up.

“Why am I doing this?”

My phone remained silent.

I opened a game instead.

That worked for about twenty minutes.

Then I got bored.

I wandered into the kitchen.

My mother was there.

“How was school?”

“Fine.”

“Anything happen?”

I almost said yes.

Instead I opened the fridge.

“No.”

She nodded.

That was the end of the conversation.

I grabbed a drink and went back to my room.

I sat at my desk and stared at my homework.

I did maybe three questions.

Then I got distracted.

Then I remembered I had a test coming up.

Then I decided I would study later.

I knew perfectly well what “later” meant.

It meant tonight.

Then tomorrow.

Then suddenly it was the night before the test and I was wondering why I'd been given an education in the first place.

I opened my notebook again.

My phone buzzed.

I froze.

I looked at the screen.

Unknown number.

For a second I didn't open it.

Then I did.

You looked happy today.

I stared at it.

Another message arrived.

Enjoy it while you can.

My stomach tightened.

I blocked the number.

Then I put my phone face down.

I told myself it was probably someone messing with me.

It was probably nothing.

I hated that phrase.

Probably nothing.

It could mean anything.

I went back to my homework.

For the next ten minutes, I didn't read a single word.

That night, I ate dinner.

I watched something on my phone.

I argued with Daniel over text about something completely stupid.

He sent me a terrible meme.

I told him it was terrible.

He said I had no taste.

I sent one back.

He stopped replying.

Victory.

It felt good.

Small things like that mattered more than they probably should have.

Maybe that was the problem.

I had a lot of small things.

Small wins.

Small embarrassments.

Small reasons to get angry.

Small reasons to laugh.

And sometimes one bad thing could make all of them feel insignificant.

But not always.

Sometimes I could forget.

Sometimes I could just be me.

I liked those moments.

I wanted more of them.

I just didn't really know how to make them happen.

I finished my homework eventually.

Mostly.

I put everything away and got ready for bed.

Before sleeping, I checked my phone one last time.

Nothing.

I stared at the screen.

Then I turned it off.

For a moment, I thought about last night.

The room.

The darkness.

The feeling that something had been there.

My chest tightened.

I told myself it had been a nightmare.

That made sense.

Nightmares made more sense than anything else.

I wasn't going to sit there inventing monsters.

I wasn't that stupid.

I got into bed.

The room was quiet.

I pulled the blanket up.

Tomorrow was Thursday.

I had school.

Daniel would probably annoy me.

Maya would probably complain about something.

I'd probably put off studying again.

Nothing had changed.

That thought should have made me feel better.

It did.

For a little while.

I closed my eyes.

And slept.

Chapter One — The Weight of Normalcy
Jonah woke because he heard something.

He didn't know what it was.

For a few seconds, he stayed still with his eyes closed, listening.

The house was quiet.

Not silent. Houses were never completely silent. There was the low hum of the fan, something ticking faintly inside the wall, the occasional sound of a vehicle passing somewhere beyond the street.

Then he heard it again.

A soft scrape.

Jonah opened his eyes.

Nothing.

The room was completely black.

He blinked.

Still nothing.

Usually there was enough light from outside to make out the curtains, the wardrobe, the edge of his desk. Tonight there wasn't even that.

He couldn't see his hand in front of his face.

Power's out.

That was his first thought.

Then he remembered the streetlights outside.

Something about that didn't make sense.

Jonah tried to turn over.

His body didn't move.

He frowned.

He tried again.

Nothing.

For a moment he wondered if he was still asleep.

He could feel the mattress underneath him. The blanket against his chest. The damp warmth at the back of his neck.

He could hear the fan.

He could hear the traffic outside.

He could swallow.

He just couldn't move.

Jonah's heart began to beat harder.

He tried lifting his right hand.

Nothing.

His left.

Nothing.

He pushed against the mattress with his shoulder.

Nothing.

A small breath escaped through his nose.

He tried to speak.

“...Mum?”

The word barely existed.

His throat had produced something, but it sounded so weak that he wasn't sure he'd actually said it.

He swallowed.

Tried again.

“Ma?”

Nothing answered.

Jonah stared into the darkness.

He couldn't see the door.

He couldn't see the ceiling.

He couldn't see anything.

Then the sound came again.

A scrape.

This time it was closer.

Jonah's breathing stopped.

He listened.

Nothing.

His heartbeat filled the room.

He tried moving his fingers.

He concentrated on his right hand.

Move.

Nothing.

Move.

His fingers remained still.

Something made a faint sound near the doorway.

Not a footstep.

More like something brushing against the floor.

Jonah's eyes moved toward it.

He couldn't see the doorway, but he knew where it was.

He had slept in this room for years.

He knew the position of everything.

The door was three or four meters away.

The wardrobe was to his left.

The desk was near the window.

The thing making that sound was somewhere between them.

Jonah stared into the blackness.

A shape appeared.

He wasn't sure it had.

He blinked.

There was nothing.

He kept looking.

Then he saw it again.

Something low to the floor.

His mind immediately tried to make sense of it.

A person.

Someone crouching.

Maybe his mother.

Maybe someone had entered the room.

Jonah tried to move.

Nothing.

The shape shifted.

Jonah's stomach tightened.

It wasn't standing.

It wasn't crouching either.

It seemed to be moving forward without changing height.

Slowly.

He couldn't hear footsteps.

Only the faint drag of something against the floor.

Jonah wanted to close his eyes.

He couldn't.

The shape came closer.

He could see a little more of it now.

Not enough.

Something pale caught the weak light from somewhere outside.

A face.

Maybe.

Jonah stared.

The shape stopped.

He couldn't make out its features.

He couldn't even tell which direction it was facing.

Then it moved its head.

Slowly.

Too slowly.

Jonah's entire body tensed.

He tried to scream.

His throat closed.

Nothing came out.

The thing remained there.

Looking at him.

Or perhaps Jonah only thought it was looking at him.

He couldn't see eyes.

He couldn't see a mouth.

He couldn't see enough to know.

The darkness seemed to swallow the rest.

Jonah's breathing became shallow.

The thing moved again.

Closer.

A hand appeared.

It touched the floor.

The fingers were pale.

Jonah stared at them.

They looked almost normal.

Then one finger bent.

Jonah's stomach dropped.

It bent farther than it should have.

He squeezed his eyes shut.

For a second, there was nothing.

Then something made a soft sound beside the bed.

Jonah opened his eyes.

The shape was gone.

He stared into the darkness.

Nothing.

He couldn't tell whether he was relieved.

Then he felt something near his ankle.

Jonah's whole body jerked.

This time, he moved.

He shot upright so violently that his shoulder struck the wall.

He screamed.

The sound came out raw and loud.

The room was empty.

Jonah scrambled backward until his back hit the headboard.

He stared at the doorway.

Closed.

He looked around.

The wardrobe.

Desk.

Curtains.

Everything was where it should have been.

His breathing came too fast.

He reached for his phone.

His hand knocked it from the bedside table.

It hit the floor.

The screen lit up.

3:17.

Jonah stared at the time.

Then at the door.

Then back at the phone.

His hands were shaking.

He climbed out of bed and switched on the light.

Nothing happened.

He froze.

The power was out.

Jonah stood there in the darkness with his phone lighting one small patch of the room.

He looked toward the floor.

Nothing.

No person.

No pale face.

No hands.

Nothing.

He checked the door.

Locked.

He remembered locking it before going to sleep.

He checked again.

Still locked.

Jonah stayed awake until morning.

At 6:11, his alarm went off.

Jonah reached under his pillow and stopped it.

For a moment he didn't move.

Morning light had returned.

The room looked normal.

That somehow made everything worse.

The crack above his wardrobe was still there. His uniform was hanging over the back of his chair. His schoolbag was on the floor where he'd dropped it.

Nothing had happened.

Nothing that could leave a mark, anyway.

Jonah sat up.

He looked at the door.

Then away.

“Bad dream.”

His voice sounded strange.

He said it again, quieter.

“Just a bad dream.”

He got dressed.

In the bathroom, he brushed his teeth while checking his phone.

Six notifications.

Four were from school groups he'd muted.

One was an advert.

The last was from an unknown number.

You awake?

Jonah stared at it.

He checked the number.

Nothing.

No name.

No profile picture.

He locked his phone.

Then unlocked it again.

The message was still there.

He blocked the number and put the phone away.

His mother was already in the kitchen.

“You're late.”

Jonah looked at the clock.

“It's 6:26.”

“You're supposed to leave before seven.”

“I know.”

She put a plate on the table.

Two slices of bread.

Jonah sat down.

“There's no milk,” she said.

“Okay.”

“You'll have to buy some when you come back.”

“Okay.”

She picked up her phone.

Jonah ate.

The bread stuck to the roof of his mouth.

His mother looked up.

“You hear me?”

“Yes.”

“Then don't forget.”

“I won't.”

She nodded and looked back at her phone.

Jonah finished eating.

He stood.

“I'm going.”

“Hmm.”

He waited.

Nothing else came.

He picked up his bag.

“Bye.”

“Bye.”

She didn't look up.

The walk to school took twenty minutes.

Jonah usually took twenty-three.

He was early.

He didn't know why.

The street was already busy. A bus rolled past with its doors open, the conductor leaning halfway out and shouting for passengers. A woman swept water away from the front of her shop. Someone had left a pile of empty bottles beside a drain.

Normal.

Jonah tried to focus on that.

His phone vibrated.

He pulled it out.

You awake?

The same number.

He stopped walking.

For a second, he simply stared at it.

Then he blocked the number again.

He put the phone away and continued.

At the school gate, two boys from his class were standing beside the security post.

One looked at Jonah.

The other leaned closer.

They said something.

Jonah kept walking.

“Jonah.”

He stopped.

Daniel stood behind him.

“What's up?”

Daniel shrugged.

“Nothing.”

Jonah waited.

Daniel looked somewhere past his shoulder.

“Never mind.”

He walked away.

Jonah watched him go.

Then he entered the school.

The classroom was loud until Jonah walked in.

Not silent.

Just quieter.

A chair scraped.

Someone laughed.

Then stopped.

Jonah went to his desk.

The boy beside him moved his bag from the other chair.

Jonah sat down.

“Morning.”

“Morning.”

The teacher came in.

Nobody said anything about the messages.

Nobody needed to.

Jonah could feel phones appearing whenever the teacher turned toward the board.

His own phone buzzed inside his pocket.

He ignored it.

It buzzed again.

He checked beneath the desk.

A screenshot.

The same accusation from the night before.

Someone had reposted it.

The wording had changed.

The story had changed with it.

Jonah read it once.

Then locked his phone.

“Jonah.”

He looked up.

“Yes, sir?”

“Are you following?”

“Yes.”

The teacher watched him for another second.

“Good.”

He turned back toward the board.

Jonah looked down.

His pen hadn't moved.

He forced himself to start writing.

By lunch, he was hungry.

He sat beneath the covered walkway behind one of the buildings.

It was quieter there.

He opened his container.

Rice and stew.

He ate.

A group of students passed.

One looked at him.

Another whispered.

The first laughed.

Jonah kept eating.

His phone vibrated.

Unknown number.

He opened it.

You should watch your back.

Jonah stared at the message.

He looked around.

The walkway was almost empty.

A teacher stood at the far end talking to two students. A security guard was smoking beside the gate.

Nobody was looking at him.

Jonah typed:

Who is this?

He stared at the words.

Then deleted them.

He put the phone away.

His appetite was gone.

He closed the container.

Rain started before the last period ended.

By the time school finished, water was already running along the road.

Jonah waited beneath the awning.

Students crowded around the entrance.

Someone complained about the rain.

Someone else called their father.

A girl beside Jonah laughed at something on her phone.

His phone vibrated.

His mother.

Where are you?

School.

The reply came immediately.

Come home.

Jonah looked at the rain.

Okay.

When it eased, he left.

He got home at 6:03.

His mother was in the living room.

“You're late.”

“There was rain.”

“You couldn't call?”

“My phone was on silent.”

She looked at him.

“You always have an excuse.”

Jonah said nothing.

He took his bag upstairs.

The television volume increased behind him.

He closed his bedroom door.

Dropped his bag.

Sat on the bed.

His phone was still in his hand.

He checked the unknown number.

Blocked.

The school group.

Muted.

The post.

Still there.

He stared at it for a while.

Then closed it.

He opened a video.

Watched half of it.

Closed it.

Opened another.

Closed that too.

At 8:14, his mother called him for dinner.

He went downstairs.

“How was school?”

“Fine.”

“How was your test?”

“Fine.”

“Did you study?”

“A little.”

She nodded.

They ate.

Neither of them spoke again.

At 12:41, Jonah was still awake.

He'd been trying to sleep for nearly an hour.

He turned onto his side.

Pulled the blanket higher.

Checked the door.

Locked.

He checked his phone.

12:42.

He put it face down beside the bed.

The house settled around him.

A pipe clicked.

Something moved downstairs.

A car passed outside.

Then nothing.

Jonah opened his eyes.

He stared at the ceiling.

The crack above the wardrobe was barely visible.

He remembered the room from the night before.

The darkness.

The shape.

The hand.

He told himself not to think about it.

He closed his eyes.

The house was quiet.

He waited.

Nothing happened.

His breathing slowed.

His thoughts became less clear.

And then he heard the scrape again.

Jonah opened his eyes.

He couldn't see anything.

He tried to move.

Nothing happened.

His heart slammed against his ribs.

He tried again.

Nothing.

The room was completely black.

No streetlight.

No moonlight.

No phone.

Nothing.

He could hear his own breathing.

Then something breathed from somewhere in the room.

Jonah stopped.

He listened.

There it was again.

Not beside him.

Not at the door.

Somewhere in the darkness.

A slow, wet breath.

Jonah tried to turn his head.

He couldn't.

Something shifted across the floor.

He couldn't see it.

He couldn't tell where it was.

The sound stopped.

Silence.

Jonah stared into the blackness.

Then, very close to his bed, something whispered his name.

“Jonah.”

His eyes widened.

And this time, he knew the voice wasn't his mother's.
